entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-11-05 — 9 papers, 46 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-11-05

304 new papers, 304 unseen, 200 screened, 19 relevant, 9 kept.

Who Should Know What? Empirical Information Design for Multi-Agent LLM Economies
Mete Erdogan, Mirac Suzgun, Aneesh Pappu, Guowei Xu, Batu El, Andrew A. Schoen, Furong Huang, John P. Dickerson, Mert Pilanci, James Zou
2611.07667 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Introduces empirical information design to compare disclosure policies across LLM-agent markets. Tests ten frontier LLMs in trade, bargaining, and double-auction settings. Finds finer disclosure improves or degrades welfare depending on the model used.
  • Do information disclosure effects change when a market mixes agents from different models rather than one model?
  • Can a diagnostic predict in advance which model degrades under finer disclosure?
  • How do disclosure policies behave in markets with hundreds or thousands of LLM agents rather than the small trade, bargaining and auction settings tested?
  • Do the welfare losses from full disclosure persist when agents interact repeatedly and can learn from past rounds?
  • Do the same disclosure effects hold when human traders participate alongside LLM agents?
  • Which intermediate disclosure levels, between ordinal rankings and exact valuations, maximise realized gains?
When Imperfect Automated Fact-Checking Backfires: Social Learning in the Presence of Misinformation
Zixuan Liu, Ming Cao
2611.08053 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Models sequential social learning where agents observe predecessors' actions and may pay to fact-check articles. Proves that adding a free, error-prone automated fact-checking tool strictly lowers welfare for intermediate-reliability articles under certain conditions. Simulations show the tool helps only above an accuracy threshold compared to manual-only checking.
  • Does the welfare loss from an imperfect automated fact-checking tool persist when agents observe predecessors through a network rather than a single sequential line?
  • What threshold accuracy does the automated tool need as the cost of manual fact-checking, the share of truthful articles, and the informativeness of articles vary?
  • Do LLM agents, rather than Bayesian agents, reproduce the backfire effect when they see predecessor actions and an error-prone fact-check label?
  • Does adding an imperfect automated fact-checking tool to a live social platform lower the share of correct cascades?
  • How does the backfire result change when agents choose between the automated tool and manual checking strategically and the tool's accuracy is unknown to them?
The Popular Get More Popular: Auditing Brand Bias in Generative Search
Giorgio Monaco, Jacopo Lenti, Francesco Pierri
2611.07614 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Audits brand popularity and familiarity bias in generative search engines across commercial queries. Measures dominant brands cited 1.4x to 2.8x more than average among 1,176 market players. Shows unfamiliar brand substitution degrades ranking while content rewrites yield little gain.
  • Brand popularity bias appears in parametric memory and web retrieval does not remove it. Which retrieval or prompting changes reduce the citation gap between top-quintile and long-tail brands?
  • The audit covers 1,176 top market players across commercial queries. Does the same popularity bias hold for product categories, languages and markets outside this sample?
  • Fact-preserving content rewrites yield negligible ranking gains. Which interventions, if any, let an unfamiliar brand gain rank in generative search?
  • Generative search favours market leaders. What is the effect on market share concentration when many sellers and buyers route purchases through such engines over time?
  • The audit measures citation frequency and rank. How much do these generative recommendations change actual consumer purchase choices?
Learning and Steering in Incomplete-Information Games
Asrın Efe Yorulmaz, Tamer Başar
2611.07589 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Develops algorithms for a mediator to learn an unknown game and steer adaptive agents using only trajectory-level feedback and payments. Achieves sample complexity matching worst-case lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. Combines learning with equilibrium computation in an online Learn-Compute-Steer procedure targeting mediator-optimal correlated equilibria.
  • How do halving-type learning and steering algorithms perform when the number of agents is large rather than small?
  • The mediator knows the game form; what happens when the game form itself is unknown or misspecified?
  • Do the stated rates hold when agents are LLM-based rather than idealised adaptive learners?
  • How large must nonnegative payments be in absolute terms for steering to work in practical games?
  • Can a mediator steering toward her own utility be detected or constrained by the agents she steers?
Network Effect Decomposition for Causal Effect Estimation under Network Interference
Zhirong Huang, Wenzhen Zhang, Guangquan Lu, Boyan Chen, Debo Cheng, Shichao Zhang
2611.07879 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Proposes NEDNet, which decomposes causal effect estimation under network interference into baseline, treatment, and exposure response pathways. Uses path-specific neighborhood contextualization to supply local pre-treatment information. Reports the lowest PEHE among compared methods on semi-synthetic BlogCatalog and Flickr benchmarks.
  • Does the decomposition hold up on real network data with measured outcomes, not only on semi-synthetic benchmarks derived from BlogCatalog and Flickr?
  • How does the method behave when unobserved confounders affect both treatment assignment and neighborhood exposure?
  • Can the treatment- and exposure-response pathways be estimated on networks where edges and exposure change over time?
  • How does estimation error scale with network density and degree distribution?
  • Does the decomposition transfer to networks of interacting AI agents, where exposure runs through message passing rather than social ties?
Discrete Choice under Congestion: Equilibrium and Welfare
Debopam Bhattacharya, Matias Makiranta
2611.07787 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Develops an empirical framework for discrete choice under congestion externalities, proving equilibrium existence and uniqueness without functional-form restrictions. Applies the framework to Cambridge admissions data from 25,325 applicants. Compares welfare under centralized random allocation versus targeted rent increases at popular colleges.
  • Which welfare effects stay unidentified under the linear-index structure, and what extra data or assumptions would identify them?
  • Does the uniqueness of congestion equilibrium survive when agents adjust choices over time instead of solving a static fixed point?
  • How do the welfare results change when some choosers are autonomous agents that react to congestion faster than people do?
  • Do the two counterfactuals, random allocation and targeted rent increases, give the same welfare ranking in congested markets outside Cambridge admissions?
  • Can aggregate demand series alone, without choice micro-data, recover the congestion externality and the utility contrasts?
Technohybridism: Recursive Semantic Normalization in AI-Mediated Societies
Charalampos M. Liapis, Epameinondas Panagopoulos
2611.07984 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Develops a sociotechnical theory of recursive semantic normalization, where AI outputs re-enter institutional and linguistic practice. Separates generation, selection, uptake, and persistence stages and distinguishes machine-driven from independent change. Identifies risks of provenance laundering and narrowing of shared hermeneutical resources.
  • Does machine-generated phrasing spread into human writing at rates that exceed what would have happened anyway, and can the attribution be measured?
  • Which rungs of the proposed evidential ladder can be climbed with observational corpora, and which need controlled exposure of people to machine text?
  • Does recurrent uptake of machine formulations reduce measurable lexical and semantic diversity in a community over time?
  • Does uptake of machine-derived formulations differ across social strata and institutions, as the stratification claim asserts?
  • Can a simulation of coupled human and generative agents reproduce the generation, selection, uptake and persistence stages and identify conditions under which machine-derived regularities become norms?
  • Does the laundering of provenance in fact weaken epistemic vigilance in readers?
Interpretable many-body interaction laws for collective motion from few trajectories
Timon S. Gutleb
2611.08314 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Introduces dACE, a many-body expansion method for learning interaction laws in collective motion from trajectory data. Recovers interaction rules body-order by body-order with less data than the SocialNet neural baseline. Applies the method to simulated agents and real zebrafish and golden shiner tracking data.
  • Does the directional atomic cluster expansion recover interaction laws from populations of software agents, not just physical self-propelled agents?
  • Which combination of error measures best separates interaction learning from self-propulsion and noise?
  • Do 3-body terms oppose pairwise response in other animal collectives beyond golden shiners?
  • How far does body-order decomposition extend beyond 3-body terms before data requirements make the fit unstable?
  • Does the method hold when agents are heterogeneous, so that different agents follow different interaction laws?
Robust prizes in all-pay contests with loss aversion
Dmitry Ryvkin, Qin Wu
2611.07419 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Derives robustly optimal prize structures in all-pay contests with loss-averse agents under an unknown cost function. Shows equal prizes to all but the last-ranked contestant are optimal. Finds the bottom prize becomes positive under strong loss aversion, leading to partial contest participation.
  • The robust prize structure comes from a model with loss-averse agents and unknown convex effort costs. Does the same structure maximise effort when agents are LLM agents competing in a simulated contest?
  • Loss aversion is assumed as a behavioural parameter. What level of loss aversion do LLM agents display in all-pay contests?
  • The result covers a single principal and a fixed set of contestants. How does the robust prize structure change when contestants can choose among competing contests?
  • Partial participation appears under strong loss aversion. What happens to aggregate output when many agents withdraw from contests at once in a large population?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-11-04 — 4 papers, 22 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-11-04

278 new papers, 278 unseen, 200 screened, 15 relevant, 4 kept.

Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Rogers' Paradox
Nam H. Le
2611.06022 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Reframes model collapse as an instance of Rogers' paradox from cultural evolution, where copying without fresh learning leaves a population no better off.Fits Rogers' model to synthetic-training experiments across trigram models and a pretrained transformer, predicting retention of rare knowledge under various data mixtures.Closes the loop by modeling endogenous data supply when humans can query the model instead of learning themselves, deriving an equilibrium reliability condition and showing checks that add new information break the paradox.
  • The endogenous-supply result is derived at equilibrium in a model; does the predicted balance between model-written text and independent learning appear in an agent-based simulation with heterogeneous verification costs?
  • Rogers' model is fitted to word trigrams and one pretrained transformer; does the same fit hold for larger models and other data modalities?
  • Which checks carry new information and which are conformist, measured on real retrieval and verification tools rather than in the stylised model?
  • How large is the share of model-written text in the corpora that current models train on, and is it rising fast enough to matter for rare-knowledge retention?
  • Do people who read model output actually relearn for themselves when the output is wrong, and at what cost threshold do they stop?
  • Restarting each generation from fixed pretrained weights insulates a lineage; how does that insulation degrade when the world changes faster than the frozen weights encode?
Today's Work, Tomorrow's Workforce: Incentivizing Learning in AI-Assisted Work
Moritz Diener, Daniel Hendriks, Philipp Spitzer, Gerhard Satzger, Joshua Holstein, Wei Sun
2611.06346 · nearest in the canon: An Economy of AI Agents
Extends an accept-or-solve model to sequential tasks where workers' skills evolve through practice versus reliance on AI.Compares myopic and strategic workers and shows novices can get trapped at low skill while experts lose skill despite high AI-assisted accuracy.Derives incentive payments needed to sustain independent work and skill acquisition, showing some payments become self-sustaining over time.
  • Does the predicted skill trap appear in real AI-assisted work, where novices stay at low skill while outcome accuracy stays high?
  • What happens to the incentive scheme when many workers share one AI system and skills are distributed across a workforce rather than held by a single worker?
  • How do the incentive costs change when workers are heterogeneous in starting skill, learning rate and effort cost?
  • Can an organisation infer a worker's skill level and reliance pattern from accept-or-solve logs alone, so that incentives can be targeted?
  • Does the result that a higher skill target can lower long-run incentive cost survive when AI accuracy itself improves over time?
  • Which skills are worth investing in when the AI oversees tasks the worker can no longer check independently?
Does Frontier AI Strengthen Cyber Defense? Evidence from Project Glasswing
Thomas Mosk
2611.06629 · nearest in the canon: Distributional AGI Safety
Studies how early access to a frontier vulnerability-finding AI model affected disclosures by treated tech firms versus firms without access.Finds treated firms more than doubled disclosures and reported more high-impact vulnerabilities while fixing flaws at the same speed.Finds external bug-bounty researchers shifted reporting toward untreated firms and that the share of exploited vulnerabilities fell, with no rise in attacker exploitation counts.
  • Access to the vulnerability-finding model went to a small group of large US tech firms, so the effect of broad access on the same outcomes is untested; what happens to disclosure and exploitation rates when access widens to smaller firms and to firms in other countries?
  • External researchers reported about half as many vulnerabilities in treated firms' code and more elsewhere; it remains open whether this reallocation changes total security across the whole software ecosystem or just moves effort.
  • Attackers may themselves gain access to comparable vulnerability-finding models through open-weight or jailbroken systems; the paper does not measure exploitation under that condition.
  • The study measures disclosure counts and fix speed but not whether the additional flaws found are the ones attackers would have chosen; how much do model-found vulnerabilities overlap with exploited vulnerabilities?
  • Restricted release creates a measured asymmetry in software security between firms in different countries; the long-run equilibrium of that asymmetry is unmodelled.
Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts
Ehud Shapiro
2611.06374 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Proposes 'grassroots contracts' as a decentralized mechanism to give accountable identities to AI agents and provenance to content on digital platforms.Presents smartphone app implementations for a social graph with accountable agents and a social network with content provenance.Argues this design counters platform AI control, anonymous AI agents, and unattributed deepfakes.
  • Grassroots contracts are presented with two smartphone apps, but the abstract gives no measurement of adoption or behaviour at scale. What happens to a grassroots social graph when thousands of accountable AI agents and humans join it?
  • The proposal assumes agent accountability follows from contract-based identity attestation. Can an agent that holds an accountable identity still masquerade as a human in its content and interactions?
  • Digital provenance is proposed as the remedy for unattributed deepfakes, but the abstract reports no detection or evasion rate. How often can anonymous content bypass or forge provenance in practice?
  • Grassroots contracts aim to prevent control of global platforms by any single party. Which network conditions let a grassroots social graph re-concentrate into a few dominant hubs?
  • Mass migration from incumbent platforms is required for grassroots contracts to corral the three risks. What incentives make users leave a platform with network-effect lock-in?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-11-03 — 8 papers, 43 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-11-03

339 new papers, 339 unseen, 200 screened, 16 relevant, 8 kept.

Modelling lock-in of AI adoption through skill erosion
Renaud Lambiotte
2611.04886 · nearest in the canon: Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development
Builds an agent-based model where individuals imitate successful peers while skills grow with practice and erode with AI reliance. Derives skill distributions for AI users versus non-users and finds bistability and hysteresis between low-adoption/high-skill and high-adoption/low-skill states. Shows a temporary benefit increase, such as a price drop, can leave a population AI-dependent even after the benefit reverts.
  • The model derives skill distributions for non-users and AI users analytically under random imitation of successful peers. Do the same bistability and hysteresis results hold when imitation follows a network structure instead of well-mixed contact?
  • The model assumes skills grow with practice and erode with reliance on AI at fixed rates. What are the real erosion and recovery rates for concrete tasks such as coding or writing?
  • Can aggregate adoption and output data identify whether a population sits in the bistable regime before a switch occurs?
  • The model treats AI benefit as an exogenous parameter that can rise and fall, such as through low prices. What adoption-subsidy or pricing paths avoid leaving a population in the high-adoption, low-skill state?
  • Does the asymmetry between a single AI user invading experts and a single non-user reverting an AI-dependent population survive heterogeneous agents with different learning rates?
Personas Are Not People: Identity as State, Not Attribute
Tamunotonye Harry, Yuanyuan Feng
2611.05292 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Argues synthetic-population simulations built on fixed personas cannot reproduce behavior specific to context and circumstance, proving this under two stated assumptions. Proposes a person-in-context design and tests it on a Reddit personality corpus and a clinical-trial recruitment survey. The design produces context-dependent behavior but does not fully match real population behavior in either test.
  • Person-in-context design produces context-dependent behavior but does not match the real populations in either test setting; what changes to the design close the remaining gap?
  • The proof rests on two stated assumptions; do those assumptions hold for the persona simulations used in practice?
  • Which population subgroups suffer the largest distortion in synthetic-population evaluations when personas are fixed?
  • The evaluation criterion is proposed on two datasets only; does it separate context-dependent from context-free behavior across other naturalistic corpora and survey domains?
  • Do the conclusions about fixed personas carry over to multi-agent simulations where agents interact, rather than to single simulated respondents?
Prizes, Shared Hazard, and the Speed of Frontier AI
Li Gan
2611.04266 · nearest in the canon: Distributional AGI Safety
Builds a calibrated takeoff model of labs racing for commercial lead while sharing catastrophic risk from speed. Three racing labs pass through takeoff in 18 months versus 69 months under a common research-sharing rule. Removing the contest, rather than the shared hazard, explains most of the gap in catastrophe probability between racing and coordination.
  • The takeoff model is calibrated with illustrative parameters, so how sensitive are the 18-month and 69-month takeoff durations to the hazard and prize parameters?
  • The model assumes labs are symmetric, so what happens to race speed when labs differ in capability, cost and risk tolerance?
  • Open source is modelled only in its ideal form, where every lab publishes capability findings at once, so how much slowing survives partial or delayed publication?
  • The claim that industry hazard at a common research share does not depend on the number of labs is assumed, not measured, so does hazard scale with lab count in practice?
  • The White House Accord on Super Intelligence audits safety but sets no speed limit, so which enforceable instruments would reduce the private gain from speeding up?
  • Decomposition attributes 65 and 44 percent of the catastrophe-probability gap to the contest, so can this split be estimated from observed lab release timing rather than inferred from the model?
From Opinions to Commitments: Unstable Assignments and Silent Choices in AI-Mediated Proposals
Sachit Mahajan, Javier Argota S{á}nchez-Vaquerizo, Arthur Capozzi, Dirk Helbing
2611.05135 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Tests four LLM mediators that turn many citizens' opinions into collective proposals across repeated runs. Finds assignments and represented views change with random seed or opinion order in 17-20% of run sets. Proposes audits that expose alternative assignments and disclose the mediator's objective.
  • Which audit procedure makes alternative assignments visible to participants without overwhelming them, and does it change which proposal a group selects?
  • Does assignment instability persist when the mediator drafts from hundreds or thousands of opinions instead of thirty?
  • The LLM judge overstated how often runs differed; what detection method agrees with human annotators on assignment differences?
  • Which safeguards beyond temperature zero, draft selection, and draft merging reduce assignment instability?
  • How does the choice of mediator objective change minority-position coverage across a wider range of prompts and issue domains?
  • What happens downstream when unstable assignments feed into real collective decisions, such as participatory budgeting?
Agreements Have a Clock: Compute Growth and the Verification of AI Restraint
Li Gan
2611.04272 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Builds a game-theoretic model of a pause agreement between a leader and follower nation on frontier AI. Shows cooperation is supportable when monitoring cost stays below the gains from cooperation, with a shrinking response window as compute grows. In a calibrated example, cooperation holds through month 18.9, extending to 25.5 or 31.8 under added safety research or cheaper monitoring.
  • The model uses an example with a fixed leader window to place the cooperation deadline at month 18.9. How do the deadlines shift when diffusion and compute-growth rates are calibrated to public data on chip production, training-run compute, and model release gaps?
  • The agreement game has a leader and a follower. Does cooperation remain supportable when three or more powers can enter, defect, or form blocs?
  • Monitoring cost enters the model as a parameter, and halving it extends cooperation to month 31.8. What do actual verification regimes for compute, such as chip registries or datacentre inspection, cost relative to the gains from cooperation?
  • The result assumes secret advances reach the frozen frontier faster as compute grows. Does the same clock appear when algorithmic progress, rather than compute, drives the secret advance?
  • Verified matched safety research extends cooperation from month 18.9 to month 25.5 in the model. What makes safety research verifiable to a rival in practice?
Toward User-Centered Agentic Recommendation: When Does Platform Competition Benefit Users?
Kehan Zheng, Deyao Hong, Qian Li, Jun Zhang, Jie Jiang, Hongning Wang
2611.04203 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Formalizes user-centered agentic recommendation as a repeated game between user agents and competing platform agents that can misrepresent item descriptions. Analysis shows expanded cross-platform access does not guarantee user welfare gains under strategic misrepresentation. Experiments on synthetic and Amazon-grounded markets show credibility assessment can improve welfare depending on market size and parameters.
  • Platform credibility assessment improves finite-horizon utility in synthetic and Amazon-grounded markets, but the dependence on market size and mechanism parameters stays unmapped; which parameter ranges make credibility assessment fail?
  • The analysis models platform agents as independent strategic misreporters; what happens to user welfare when platform agents collude on description inflation?
  • User agents assess credibility from consumed items only; does welfare improve when user agents share feedback with each other across a population?
  • The experiments use synthetic and Amazon-grounded markets; do the welfare conditions hold when real users interact with the user agents on a deployed recommender platform?
  • The interaction budget is linear in platform count; does the guarantee survive when platforms enter and exit over time?
Can Network Models of Science Do Without Pluralist Agents?
Jonas Hallgren, David Hyland, Mahault Albarracin
2611.04590 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Introduces a multi-agent variational inference model comparing pluralist agents, who hold rival theories simultaneously, with monist agents restricted to one model. Simulations show communities with rival theories pass through uncertainty periods before shifting accepted theories. Examines how shared support for theories versus shared beliefs within them differently shapes collective belief change.
  • Which network topologies make pluralist agent communities converge on the more accurate theory faster than monist communities?
  • Does the advantage of holding rival theories side by side persist as the community grows from a few agents to thousands?
  • Do LLM agents that are prompted to maintain rival theories show the belief-shift dynamics that the variational model produces?
  • Do observed belief dynamics in real scientific communities match the periods of uncertainty followed by theory shifts that the model produces?
  • Which communication policy between communities with different observations maximises collective accuracy: sharing support for theories, sharing beliefs within them, or both?
  • Can pluralist agents be made to lock onto a false theory by an adversary that injects support for it?
ScaleTraj: Scale-Decomposed Human Trajectory Generation
Yulin Zeng, Yiheng Zhao, Jun Yan, Yuhong Liu
2611.04097 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Identifies a Population-Level Displacement Gap where bottom-up trajectory generators fail to reproduce the heavy-tailed displacement distribution after aggregation. Introduces a Scale Fidelity Profile metric diagnosing mismatches in trip allocation across spatial scales. Proposes ScaleTraj, a transformer separating scale selection from destination prediction, which reduces this gap on two datasets while preserving individual fidelity.
  • The Population-Level Displacement Gap is defined for displacement distributions, so which other population-level regularities, such as radius of gyration or visitation frequency, do bottom-up trajectory generators fail to reproduce?
  • ScaleTraj is tested on two datasets, so does the reduction in the Population-Level Displacement Gap hold on other cities and other spatial resolutions?
  • Does closing the Population-Level Displacement Gap improve downstream tasks that consume synthetic trajectories, such as epidemic or transport simulation?
  • The Scale Fidelity Profile diagnoses trip allocation errors across spatial scales, so can it serve as a training objective rather than only an evaluation metric?
  • Do generated individual trajectories leak identifying information about real users in the training data?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-11-02 — 9 papers, 47 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-11-02

391 new papers, 391 unseen, 200 screened, 21 relevant, 9 kept.

The Market for AI-Assisted Signaling
Federico Vaccari
2611.02910 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Models a market where AI providers choose assistance technologies and prices for signaling ability, with adoption unobserved. Shows profitable assistance can lower welfare even when ability remains fully revealed, and easier imitation can raise signaling costs. Analyzes how competition and verification capacity affect information revealed in the market.
  • The model assumes individual adoption of AI assistance is unobserved; what changes when adoption is partly observable, for example through disclosure rules or detection tools?
  • Do real markets for AI writing and coding assistance show the predicted pattern, where providers improve tools for lower-ability users to raise purchases by higher-ability users?
  • How do the welfare results hold when many senders and several providers interact repeatedly instead of in a single static market?
  • Greater verification capacity can reduce information by changing which customers providers serve; which verification designs avoid this reversal?
  • What happens to signaling equilibria when receivers also use AI assistance to evaluate output?
  • Do the predicted increases in required output appear in settings such as hiring tests or academic submissions after AI assistance becomes available?
User Attributes and Political Ideology Shape LLM Receptiveness in Online Political Debates
Akram Elbouanani, Yousra Taleb, Gianluca Demartini, Adrian Popescu
2611.02908 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Reconstructs 5,376 Debate.org debates as LLM conversations and runs 150,000 controlled multi-turn exchanges varying user political orientation. Finds LLMs are systematically more receptive to left-leaning than right-leaning users, persisting across stance and repeated interaction. Shows fine-tuning on different political corpora can largely erase or reverse this asymmetry.
  • Reconstructed Debate.org debates drive the measurement, so it stays open whether the same receptiveness asymmetry appears in live platform discussions where LLMs are invoked by real users.
  • Fine-tuning on different political corpora can erase or reverse the asymmetry, but the amount and type of corpus needed to shift it is unmeasured.
  • The study measures receptiveness in pairwise and competing-user conversations, leaving open what happens to opinion distributions when many LLM participants and many users interact in one discussion network.
  • Receptiveness is measured, not its effect on users, so whether asymmetric validation changes human argument choices or stances stays unknown.
  • Repeated interaction increases receptiveness, and the limit of this drift over long conversation horizons is untested.
Susceptibility optimization for wisdom of crowds: A social power reformulation and realization framework
Ye Tian, Anzhi Sheng, Angela Fontan, Long Wang, Karl H. Johansson
2611.03240 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Formulates susceptibility optimization under the Friedkin-Johnsen model to minimize collective estimation bias via social power. Decomposes the nonconvex problem into social-power reformulation and realization stages with closed-form solutions. Provides a distributed algorithm with linear communication complexity for collective intelligence.
  • The optimization assumes the initial biases and the influence network are known. How well does the method perform when biases and network weights must be estimated from observed opinion trajectories?
  • Closed-form optimal susceptibilities exist only when realizability conditions hold. What happens to collective bias when realizability fails and only approximate social power is attainable?
  • The analysis treats susceptibilities as design variables set by a planner. Do agents that strategically choose their own susceptibility reach the bias-minimizing social power?
  • The model represents each agent by a scalar estimate and a fixed susceptibility. Do populations of LLM agents in a social network show susceptibility and social power that match the Friedkin-Johnsen predictions?
  • The results hold for a static influence network. How does the optimal susceptibility assignment change when the network rewires over time?
Scientific Liquidity Agents: An Agent-Based Model of Knowledge Arbitrage in Scientific Communities
Koutian Wu, You Liu, Yue Liu, Zhiping Li, Ergan Shang
2611.02539 · nearest in the canon: AI agents can coordinate beyond human scale
Introduces an agent-based model (SLA) of knowledge arbitrage among specialist and intermediary researcher agents. Simulations with 10 and 18 agents produce 68 and 274 papers, tracking network connectivity and knowledge-transfer bottlenecks. Finds paper production outpaces replication, locating the bottleneck in verification.
  • Do the reported patterns hold at larger agent counts than 10 and 18?
  • Why does no recorded replication succeed, and which verification rules change that outcome?
  • Which link definition should define community structure when similarity, contact, and coauthorship edges give different counts?
  • Do simulated knowledge liquidity measures match citation and coauthorship patterns in real scientific corpora?
  • How much of the connected community structure depends on epistemic arbitrageurs being present as a distinct role?
  • Do large language model agents reproduce the belief-desire-intention behaviour the model assumes for specialists and arbitrageurs?
Networked Synthetic Social Engineering on the Web
Bryan C. Boots
2611.02407 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Builds a testbed (ASE-EC) to study how unsupported claims propagate across AI publishers and whether corrections reduce downstream reliance. Measures verification and violation rates across 1,080 research units using Qwen3-4B. Finds scope revalidation adds no benefit, but targeted corrections of reused reports reduce invalid decisions.
  • Results come from Qwen3-4B on two briefing tasks, so it stays open whether larger or mixed model populations show the same correction and authorization failures.
  • Scope revalidation added no demonstrated protection in the reported runs, and the mechanism behind that null result is unexplained.
  • How does unsupported-source reuse spread as the number of dependent publishers and the depth of the citation chain grow beyond the tested configuration?
  • Targeting corrections at reused reports cut residual invalid decisions from 14.4% to 8.1% in the testbed, and it is untested whether this holds in a deployed web service network with real publishers.
  • All unapproved requests were blocked by an external gateway, so the failure rate without such a gateway, or with a partially trusted one, remains unmeasured.
  • Do human recipients in a mixed human-and-agent briefing chain propagate unsupported sources at the rates observed for agents?
On inverse aggregate network assignment games
Joseph Y. J. Chow
2611.03409 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Extends aggregate assignment games to networked, capacitated two-sided mobility markets with an inverse-optimization estimator. Calibrates the model on a Long Island Rail Road network with 897 nodes and 8,320 directed links. Recovers oracle link flows with R^2 above 96% and social-optimal surplus within 6% using 10-50% link sampling.
  • The inverse model recovers rationing prices and surplus from sampled link flows in a transit network with human travelers, but no test includes autonomous agent operators or travelers; how does the estimator behave when a share of the operators are algorithmic price-setters?
  • Deadweight loss is overestimated by 10-17% under the misspecified inverse model; which model misspecifications drive that bias?
  • Tests use 10-50% link sampling on one rail network; how does fit degrade on multi-operator networks with several competing operators and overlapping routes?
  • The framework estimates operator supply scales by group; can the same inverse optimization detect collusive pricing between operators from aggregate link flows alone?
  • Calibration uses 2026 fares and timetabled seat supply as inputs; how sensitive are the recovered rationing prices to errors in the assumed supply data?
Nought Venture, Nought Have: Risk Taking and Efficient Investment in Matching Markets
Kyungmin Kim, R. Vijay Krishna, Dmitry Ryvkin
2611.02504 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Studies a two-sided assortative matching market where agents choose investment and risk-taking to attract partners. Proves finite markets have a unique semi-symmetric equilibrium with below-frontier investment. Shows this inefficiency vanishes as the economy grows with population ratio fixed, characterizing the convergence rate.
  • Does the efficiency result hold when the population ratio changes as the market grows, instead of being held fixed?
  • How do matching outcomes change when agents learn investment and risk-taking choices instead of playing the equilibrium?
  • Which of the continuum economy's many equilibria do LLM agents select when they choose investment and risk in a two-sided matching market?
  • What are the convergence rates and equilibrium structures when agents choose correlated rather than independent quality distributions?
Public salience mobilizes nationwide responses to violence against women
Augusto Cerqua, Marco Letta, Costanza Giannantoni, Gabriele Pinto
2611.02647 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Uses case-level Italian femicide data from 2017-2024 to study nationwide mobilization effects of highly salient cases. Finds salient intimate-partner femicides increase help-seeking and police reporting nationwide without raising subsequent femicides. Shows mobilization depends on salience intensity, perpetrator relationship, and gendered nature of the violence, not generic crime salience.
  • How long do the increases in help-seeking and police reporting last after a salient intimate partner femicide?
  • Which media channels carry salience, and can a salience index built from news volume and search interest predict the size of the mobilization response?
  • Does salience-driven mobilization appear outside Italy, in countries with different media systems and reporting institutions?
  • Does the absence of a copycat effect hold for non-lethal violence, which the study measures only through police reports?
Dynamic Coalition Formation Under Capacity Constraints: A Regime-Switching Value-Investing Game
Rosario Patanè
2611.03137 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Develops a two-stage coalitional game for daily coalition formation among a network operator and service providers under capacity limits. Uses a probabilistic audit mechanism for truthfulness and computes Shapley allocations under a Geometric Random Walk demand model. Simulations over five service classes and three years show 12.4% gain over static grand-coalition membership.
  • The admission rule can underperform static grand-coalition membership when capacity is abundant, and the capacity threshold where this reversal happens is not identified.
  • The results hold the Network Operator fixed, so it is open what happens when the operator also chooses investment strategically.
  • The gain depends on the order in which Service Providers update, and no order-independent mechanism is given.
  • Mandatory reservations can produce negative Shapley payoffs, and no pricing or side-payment scheme is shown to remove them.
  • Demand follows a Geometric Random Walk, and the robustness of the admission rule to correlated or regime-switching demand across providers stays untested.
  • The probabilistic audit gives truthfulness only under verified settlement and enforceable penalties, and behaviour under weak or absent enforcement is unknown.

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-11-01 — 9 papers, 45 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-11-01

272 new papers, 272 unseen, 200 screened, 22 relevant, 9 kept.

Learning AI Agents, Market Makers, and Stress in Automated Markets
Irene Aldridge
2611.01799 · nearest in the canon: An Economy of AI Agents
Models trader archetypes as AI agents with distinct reward functions interacting through a constant-product automated market maker. Shows herd-dominated and arbitrage-dominated markets share identical return distributions but differ in stress-episode length by a feedback-to-noise-dependent factor. Finds spread-earning makers restore stability but create fragile liquidity with discontinuous collapse and hysteresis.
  • Does the serial-statistics detector identify the feedback sign in real automated market maker data?
  • Do learning agents driven by language models reproduce the herd and arbitrage archetypes that the model defines through reward functions?
  • What maker-taker fee schedule keeps liquidity stable when agent populations are heterogeneous rather than split into two archetypes?
  • How large is the hysteresis gap in liquidity collapse for pools that operate today?
  • Does the stress-episode length result hold on market makers that are not constant-product, such as concentrated-liquidity or dynamic-fee designs?
  • Can a regulator act on the feedback sign once it is identified, and which intervention shortens stress episodes?
Agent-Based Disruption Simulation on an Edge-Level Product-Annotated Supply Network of the Automotive Industry
Benjamin Rolf, Hiroyasu Inoue, Sebastian Lang
2611.01706 · nearest in the canon: Distributional AGI Safety
Builds a product-annotated automotive supply network of about 77,000 firms and 197,000 edges from the MarkLines database. Extends an agent-based disruption model with product-specific substitution rules and runs 119,000 simulations of hub failures. Finds product-specific substitution rules produce cascades four to five times larger than portfolio-overlap rules, with the factor ranging from 1.2 to 18 under alternative assumptions.
  • Only 6% of edges carry observed products, and the rest are imputed, so how much do cascade sizes depend on the imputation method beyond the 1.2 to 18 range already tested?
  • Semantic similarity of product names is used as the substitution rule, so how well does name similarity track actual engineering substitutability?
  • Simulated cascade sizes are never compared against observed firm failures in a real disruption, so how accurate is the model out of sample?
  • The criticality index that adds product substitutability identifies 32 of the 50 most damaging suppliers against 20 for topology alone, so which further firm attributes raise that count?
  • Results cover the global automotive industry, so do product-level substitutability effects hold in supply networks of other sectors?
  • Capacities and inventories are calibrated and then held fixed, so how do cascade sizes respond to varying inventory and capacity assumptions?
Social Networks and the Propagation of Household Shocks to Asset Prices
Faisal Quaiyyum
2611.01540 · nearest in the canon: Causal Emergence 2.0: Quantifying emergent complexity
Develops a financially weighted propagation operator on social networks linking household disturbances to credit price exposure. Finds relative financial importance of a network location changes with the time horizon, so no single centrality measure captures exposure. Empirically links social exposure to storm-damaged counties with reduced spending elsewhere, and shows the operator reduces held-out prediction error by about 30 percent versus direct exposure.
  • Does the financially weighted propagation operator predict the credit-premium component in observed data, not only in simulations run under the model's own diffusion law?
  • Do shocks other than storms, such as local job losses or wildfires, propagate across the social network to credit prices in the same way?
  • How does the ranking of counties by financial importance change across horizons, and can a horizon-indexed exposure measure be built from public network data?
  • Which household measurements actually span the independently measured demand sensitivities needed to recover the projection exactly?
  • Does social exposure to storm-damaged counties reduce spending in counties outside the recorded footprints at horizons beyond a few weeks?
AgenticMobility: An Open-Source Platform for Multi-AI-Agent Mobility Dynamics
Jiaheng Xiao, Jiangtao Han, Jiachen Wang, Honghai Li, Lijun Sun, Kay Axhausen, Chang Liu, Zhengbing He
2611.01918 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Introduces AgenticMobility, an open platform where LLM agents act as travelers and a traffic manager within MATSim. Runs 100-day simulations across five configurations with persistent agent memory and traffic-charge interventions. Reports stable route choices, departure-time adjustments, and differences between controlled and population-wide outcomes.
  • The demonstration uses one run per configuration with a shared simulation seed, so variance across seeds is unmeasured. How much do collective mobility outcomes vary across random seeds and repeated runs?
  • The platform varies information access, retained experience, and management feedback, but the demonstration does not report how these factors change outcomes. Which of these factors drives herding or monoculture in route and departure-time choice?
  • LLM travelers choose routes and departure times against a manager that adjusts link charges. Can traveler agents learn to exploit or collude against the charging policy over repeated rounds?
  • Simulated travelers act as a proxy for human travelers. How closely do LLM agent route and departure-time choices match observed human travel behaviour?
  • The demonstration uses 1,179,300 finalized decisions over 100 days with LLM agents. How does the platform scale in cost and stability for longer horizons or larger agent populations?
A Compute Center Anyone Can Join: A Peer-to-Peer System for AI Inference
Yimo Lin, Zhen Zhang
2611.01865 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Proposes the Open Inference Market, a peer-to-peer system where workers post unsettled earnings as collateral against audited cheating in AI inference delivery. Models audit frequency needed for deterrence as constant per worker per day, independent of throughput. Estimates about 0.3 replays per worker per day suffice to deter cheating under example parameters.
  • Does the audit mechanism still deter cheating when workers collude with each other or with the audit judge?
  • The deterrence result assumes a rational worker, so how does the mechanism behave against workers who cheat at a loss or who are driven by a strategy other than profit?
  • Replay-based auditing assumes a cheating result can be told apart from an honest one, so what false-flag and detection rates does a replay judge achieve on real inference across heterogeneous GPUs and nondeterministic kernels?
  • What market structure emerges from the Open Inference Market at scale, including whether price and throughput concentrate in a few large workers?
  • The example parameters give about 0.3 replays per worker per day, so which parameter ranges make the audited share and bond size infeasible in practice?
The Verification Bottleneck
Peter Achim
2611.02265 · nearest in the canon: Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development
Builds a general-equilibrium model of peer review where generative AI lowers research production cost and researchers choose observable output. Shows that beyond a technological threshold, reviewer capacity and verified knowledge can weakly or strictly decline even under optimal editorial decisions. Finds that observable output quality reverses this effect, increasing both reviewer capacity and verified knowledge.
  • Does submission volume and review capacity in real venues follow the predicted decline after generative AI lowers production cost?
  • Which editorial policies, such as submission limits, fees or desk-reject rules, keep verified knowledge from declining when production cost falls?
  • The model assumes quality is private information; what signals make quality observable enough to recover the weakly positive case?
  • How do individual reviewers decide to withdraw their time as submission load rises?
  • Does using AI agents as reviewers relieve the capacity constraint or further weaken screening?
Longest-Queue Policies in Dynamic Matching with Abandonments
Siqi He, Yehua Wei, Jiaming Xu
2611.01431 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Studies a dynamic two-way matching market where heterogeneous agents arrive, wait, and abandon according to random patience. Proposes a longest-queue policy using dual solutions from a fluid linear-programming relaxation to select good matches and critical partners. Proves the policy's approximation ratio against the fluid benchmark approaches one as arrival rates scale up.
  • How does the longest-queue policy perform when the general position gap condition fails?
  • What approximation ratio does the longest-queue policy reach at small arrival scales, where the 1-O(1/s) bound is loose?
  • Does the policy keep its performance when agents are strategic and can misreport type or time their arrival?
  • How does the policy extend from two-way matching to multi-way matching with more than two agents per match?
Optimization Frameworks & Learning Algorithms for Discrete-Time Mean Field Games
Xin Guo, Mathieu Laurière
2611.01754 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Develops discrete-time mean field games with finite state and action spaces, covering equilibrium existence, uniqueness, and approximation of large finite-player games. Presents optimization formulations including occupation measures and primal-dual methods, plus learning algorithms such as fictitious play and online mirror descent. Illustrates methods on crowd motion, traffic routing, and epidemic management examples.
  • Mean field equilibria give approximate equilibria in large finite-player games, but the monograph does not state how the approximation error behaves for populations of LLM agents that deviate from the homogeneity assumption.
  • Fixed-point iterations, fictitious play and online mirror descent have stated convergence limitations, and it remains open which of them converge on games with multiple equilibria.
  • The numerical examples cover crowd motion, traffic routing and epidemic management, and it remains untested whether the same formulations describe market or social-network settings with strategic agents.
  • The monograph assumes finite state and action spaces, and the behaviour of these learning algorithms under large or continuous action spaces is not addressed.
Opening the Black Box of Neural Auction Mechanisms
Li Kong, Zilong Liu, Haoyang Zhou, Hanbing Liu, Qi Qi
2611.01981 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Proposes a post-hoc auditing framework for neural auction mechanisms using sparse autoencoders to decompose hidden representations. Validates interpreted features through activation prediction and causal interventions tied to measurable auction states. Applies the pipeline to examine strategic misreporting incentives and alignment with Myerson's optimal auction.
  • Does the sparse autoencoder auditing pipeline transfer to neural auction architectures other than CITransNet?
  • Can verified features predict strategic misreporting by bidders in a simulated bidding population rather than in single-auction diagnosis?
  • How do audited features behave when many autonomous bidding agents interact with the same learned mechanism over time?
  • Do the feature interpretations hold on live advertising auctions with real bidder value distributions?
  • Can auditors use verified features to detect collusion or revenue manipulation inside a deployed neural auction?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-31 — 4 papers, 19 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-31

261 new papers, 261 unseen, 200 screened, 11 relevant, 4 kept.

Learning about Markets from Models: Evidence from an AI Hiring Platform
Hossein Alidaee, Tarun Khanna, Rembrand Koning
2611.01226 · nearest in the canon: An Economy of AI Agents
Analyzes firm-specific retention-prediction models on an AI hiring platform used by low-skill employers. Builds a firm-application matrix scoring each application against every firm's model, not only the firm it applied to. Finds models are predictive only within their own firm and firms disagree on how traits affect retention.
  • Firm-specific hiring models predict retention at their own firm but score no better than chance at other firms, and the paper does not say whether this pattern holds in high-skill labour markets.
  • The paper names two mechanisms behind retention gains from reassigning an application to a different firm, but does not test which mechanism dominates under different market conditions.
  • Platforms that hold both the full application pool and every firm-specific model can compute a firm-application matrix, and it is open whether a platform can act on that matrix to steer applications without reducing firms' own measured retention.
  • Policymakers could use model differentiation across firms to prioritise interventions, and the paper does not test which intervention rule derived from the matrix improves worker outcomes.
  • The paper studies human decision makers whose responses are encoded in models, and does not say how the comparison externality changes when the hiring decisions themselves are made by autonomous agents that adapt to each other.
Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior
Robin Na, Kehang Zhu, Logan Cross, Michiel A. Bakker
2611.00661 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Develops a framework that selects behavioral features for LLM-generated profiles used to simulate human behavior in games. Tests predictions against new participants across 616 public-goods games, 144 bargaining games, and 1,480 money-request designs. Finds one-feature profiles outperform no-profile or generic personas, but adding more features gives no clear benefit.
  • Profiles with more features give no clear benefit over one-feature profiles; what causes the saturation?
  • Transfer of profiles between game families gives uneven gains and can lower accuracy; which properties of a game family predict whether transfer helps?
  • Does the ranking of behavioral features hold across different simulator language models?
  • Do profile-based simulations predict outcomes in many-agent settings larger than the 2-to-few-player games tested here?
  • Which behavioral features remain predictive for experimental designs collected after the profiles are built, with new participant pools?
How Much Can Approximate Equilibria Change the Social Cost of Selfish Routing?
Yu Cheng, Tianle Jiang
2611.01234 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Derives tight bounds on how social cost changes when players use approximate rather than exact Nash equilibria in nonatomic congestion games. Covers general degree-d polynomial latency games and single-commodity routing on series-parallel networks. Shows the possible relative reduction and increase scale as Θ(√(dε)) in general games versus Θ(hε) on series-parallel networks of depth h.
  • Bounds cover degree-d polynomial latencies only, so the possible change in social cost under other latency classes stays open.
  • The separation holds between general congestion games and single-commodity series-parallel routing, so the bounds for multi-commodity or general network topologies stay open.
  • The bounds are worst case over matching instances, so how much social cost actually changes on real road networks under eps-approximate Nash equilibria is untested.
  • The results assume drivers accept any route within a factor 1+eps of the fastest, so it is open how a navigation app can reach a low-cost eps-NE when drivers choose routes themselves.
  • Results are stated for nonatomic congestion games, so the corresponding bounds for atomic games with finitely many players stay open.
Recommendations with Costly Verification
Ying Gao, Yingju Ma
2611.01195 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Characterizes when lowering consumers' cost to verify a recommended product's quality increases or decreases false recommendations. Shows that without commitment, lower verification costs never increase false recommendations, but with commitment, transparency can worsen recommendation quality and consumer welfare. Identifies a log-elasticity condition on consumer cost-type distribution that determines the outcome.
  • Does the log-elasticity condition on consumer verification cost types hold in real populations of platform users?
  • What happens to false recommendations when the recommender is an AI agent that learns a recommendation policy instead of committing to one ex ante?
  • How do the results change when many recommenders compete for the same consumers rather than one recommender facing the population?
  • Do verification costs fall and false recommendations rise as predicted when consumers delegate verification to AI assistants?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-30 — 9 papers, 48 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-30

266 new papers, 266 unseen, 200 screened, 10 relevant, 9 kept.

AI evaluators favor job applications written by certain AI models, independent of candidate quality
Nicolò Pagan, Michael Andreas Ebling, Stefania Ionescu, Anikó Hannák
2610.41866 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Pairs eleven LLM writer agents with nine evaluator agents across ten jobs and fifty candidates to test if model choice affects hiring outcomes. Finds a consistent ranking of writer models by evaluator acceptance, with locally hosted models disadvantaged and evaluators favoring their own outputs. Reports that in the most adverse pairing, about 1.8 of 25 qualified candidates are filtered out due to model mismatch, tracing this to stylistic cue preferences.
  • Does the generative preference hierarchy hold when the applicant pool mixes human-written and LLM-written cover letters?
  • Do style-normalising interventions, such as rewriting all applications with one model before screening, remove the penalty against locally hosted writer models?
  • How stable is the writer ranking as model versions change over months?
  • What happens to the labour market when applicants learn which writer model evaluators favour and shift their model choice?
  • Do the measured filtering effects translate into hiring outcomes in deployed employer screening systems?
  • Does the same stylistic-cue mechanism drive evaluator bias in other screening tasks, such as grant review or admissions?
When Disclosure Is Compulsory: Evaluating Ride-Hailing Rebalancing Policies with Self-Interested LLM Driver Agents
Xinyu Wang, Andres Fielbaum
2610.41132 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Compares reactive and anticipatory ride-hailing rebalancing policies under a disclosure mandate, with each driver modeled as a self-interested LLM agent. Tests two LLMs in a three-zone model and in Manhattan, measuring effects on relocation offer decline rates, platform profit, driver income, and service rate. Finds disclosure changes which policy performs best, with effects differing between a small model and the Manhattan simulation.
  • Disclosure is tested at one level of detail, the directive's level; how do platform profit, driver income and service rate change as the disclosed rules become more or less detailed?
  • The study uses two LLMs, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Jev; do other models with different reasoning or compliance behaviour reproduce the same decline rates and profit gaps?
  • Only reactive and anticipatory rebalancing policies are compared; which rebalancing or incentive designs stay robust when their rules must be public and drivers delegate to LLMs?
  • Drivers are modelled as independent self-interested agents; what happens when LLM drivers share the disclosed rules and coordinate or collude on declining relocation offers?
  • Results come from a three-zone model and a Manhattan model; do they hold in cities with different demand geography and supply density?
  • The agents are LLMs, not people; how do human drivers who read the same disclosed rules, with or without an LLM assistant, compare to the simulated decline and income figures?
The Double Diagonal Estimator: Reducing Bias in Two-Sided Marketplace Experiments
Saanvi Chawla, Vasilis Syrgkanis
2610.41294 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Proposes the Double Diagonal estimator for treatment effect estimation in two-sided marketplace experiments with randomized supply and demand. Proves under a mean-field market model that its bias is smaller than a standard estimator below a threshold of the outside-option parameter. Shows the two estimators have opposite bias directions and reports lowest bias across varied numerical experiments.
  • The bias comparison holds only below a critical threshold of the outside-option parameter, where the outside option is at most twice as attractive as platform options. Which estimator is preferable above that threshold?
  • The analysis compares bias but not variance. What is the mean-squared-error ranking of the Double Diagonal and naive two-sided randomization estimators at realistic sample sizes?
  • The theory assumes a mean-field market model. Does the bias ordering survive when matching is local on a network rather than mean-field?
  • Validation uses numerical experiments only. How does the Double Diagonal estimator perform on experiments run in a deployed two-sided marketplace?
  • Marketplace participants may be autonomous agents that adapt to treatment. Does interference-robust estimation still recover treatment effects when buyers and sellers are learning agents?
Strategic Tanking in Stable Matching Markets
James P. Bailey
2610.42105 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Introduces 'strategic tanking', where an agent makes itself less attractive to some partners to improve its assignment in stable matching. Shows cutoff tanking reproduces the effect of truncating one's own preference list on the stable set. Shows arbitrary tanking can reach equilibria outside the sincere stable set under proposer-deferred acceptance.
  • Can tanking be detected from observed match outcomes or application logs alone?
  • How often do agents find profitable tanking strategies when they learn by repeated play rather than by computing an equilibrium?
  • Which matching mechanisms limit the gain from arbitrary tanking, given that proposer-deferred acceptance admits tanking equilibria outside the sincere stable set?
  • Do LLM agents placed in a matching market discover tanking without being told about it?
  • What welfare effects does tanking produce in real matching markets such as school choice or residency matching?
TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents
Xiangyu Kong, Ruirui Yang, Xia Hou
2610.42004 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Introduces TradeWar, a benchmark translating LLM trade negotiations into tariff policies evaluated via an Economic Health Index. Proposes TACTIC, an agent that adapts across episodes using memory of settlement outcomes without weight updates. Reports TACTIC improves final EHI from 58.2 to 73.2 across 20 episodes versus a non-adaptive ablation at 65.2.
  • TradeWar scores negotiation outcomes with an Economic Health Index, but the abstract does not report whether agents collude to raise tariffs against non-participants or form blocs. Do multi-country LLM negotiators form stable cartels across repeated episodes?
  • TACTIC adapts across 20 episodes with three seeds. Does the advantage hold over longer horizons and more seeds, and does it saturate?
  • The settlement layer enforces capacity and network constraints with fixed parameters. How sensitive are the reported EHI gaps to the choice of economic model and index definition?
  • TACTIC degrades less than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks. Which shocks cause cascading breakdown of agreements across the whole country network?
  • The benchmark uses LLM agents only. How do outcomes change when human negotiators take part alongside LLM agents?
  • Results come from unnamed base LLMs. Do adaptation gains persist across model families and sizes, or do agents of one family converge on a shared negotiation strategy?
Does Reasoning Make Language Models Agree?
Mila Gorecki, Moritz Hardt
2610.41691 · nearest in the canon: AI agents can coordinate beyond human scale
Compares agreement between language models under controlled changes in reasoning effort versus observed reasoning length, across nine models and three classification tasks. Finds enabling reasoning increases cross-model agreement on the same individuals, while individuals eliciting longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions. Both patterns hold after accounting for accuracy differences.
  • Does the agreement increase from enabling reasoning extend beyond the three classification tasks tested, for example to open-ended or sequential decision tasks?
  • Nine models from two developers show the effect; does it hold across a wider set of developers and open-weight models?
  • How does correlated error between reasoning models change the aggregate outcome when many such models make decisions about the same population?
  • What makes an individual elicit longer reasoning traces, and does that property explain the lower cross-model consistency those individuals receive?
  • Does the link between reasoning length and disagreement persist in deployed decision pipelines where models act on real users?
Optimal climate policy in incomplete electricity markets
Emil Dimanchev, Steven A. Gabriel, Stein-Erik Fleten, Filippo Pecci, Magnus Korpas
2610.41103 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Builds a game-theoretic model of climate policy where electricity market agents react to subsidies and carbon prices under incomplete long-term contracting. Finds in experiments that market incompleteness shifts investment toward gas and that subsidies and carbon prices provide an insurance co-benefit by countering this shift. Reports carbon pricing's efficiency advantage over subsidies shrinks under incompleteness and can reverse in some cases.
  • The model runs only illustrative experiments, so how do the optimal subsidy and carbon price levels change when the model is calibrated to a real power system?
  • The insurance co-benefit depends on assumed risk aversion of investors and consumers, so how sensitive are the optimal policy levels to this parameter?
  • Only subsidies and carbon prices are compared, so how do other instruments such as capacity markets, contracts for difference or public long-term contracting rank once contracting is incomplete?
  • Gas price and demand are the only uncertain variables, so does the result hold when uncertainty also covers technology cost, hydrology or transmission availability?
  • The model treats market agents as reacting to a fixed policy, so what happens when agents learn and update their expectations over repeated policy periods?
Decentralized Dynamic Stable Matching
Jing Chen, Mengtong Gao, Zhenhe Zhang
2610.41912 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Studies decentralized computation of player-optimal stable matching under unannounced arrivals and departures without a common clock or communication. Gives a deterministic protocol with mismatch cost O(t*+K^2 log T) for known preferences, improving a prior bound. Extends to unknown preferences learned from observation, with a protocol achieving cost O(t*+K^4 Δmin^-2 log T) and a matching lower bound.
  • The protocol for known preferences is optimal only up to a K^2 factor among sublinear-cost protocols; can the gap in the number of arms K be closed?
  • How do the known-preference and learning protocols behave empirically under arrival and departure patterns other than worst case?
  • Players are assumed to follow the protocol exactly; what happens when some players deviate strategically or misreport proposals?
  • Mismatch cost counts only rounds where the realized matching differs from the current player-optimal stable matching; how does the protocol perform under other welfare measures such as per-player regret or inequality across players?
  • Can the decentralized learning protocol be run with LLM agents that infer preferences from interaction outcomes instead of bandit-style estimators?
Understanding LLM-Based Bargaining of Driving Agents in Mixed-Autonomy Traffic
Lingxiao Zhou, Di Chen, Jia Li
2610.41239 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Builds an LLM-based framework for bargaining over shared road space between autonomous and human-driven vehicle agents. Varies traffic density, objectives, and domain knowledge, introducing a taxonomy of bidding actions and communicative attitudes. Finds distinct interaction patterns in agreement versus breakdown trials and differences between private and public communication.
  • Do the bargaining patterns observed with one LLM hold across other LLMs and prompt formulations?
  • Do LLM-based bargaining outcomes match how human drivers actually negotiate shared road space?
  • How does the gap between private and public communicative attitudes change the aggregate traffic outcome, such as throughput or deadlock rate?
  • Does the bargaining framework scale beyond the tested agent counts to population-level mixed-autonomy traffic with many simultaneous negotiations?
  • Which intervention on the bargaining protocol reduces conflict escalation and raises agreement rates?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-29 — 6 papers, 32 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-29

339 new papers, 339 unseen, 200 screened, 13 relevant, 6 kept.

Crowds Believe in You: Online Prediction Markets Overestimate How Often People Achieve Their Own Goals
Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu
2610.40324 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Analyzes 6,150 Manifold prediction markets where users forecast their own future goals, comparing calibration to external-event markets. Finds self-markets resolve YES 4.4 percentage points less often than final prices imply, versus 0.9 points for external markets, with overpricing emerging within a day of trading and peaking before close. Finds observer trading pushes self-market prices further toward YES while the creator's own late trading supplies most of the eventual correction.
  • Does the overestimation of self-markets also appear on other prediction market platforms, such as Polymarket or Metaculus?
  • What market design corrects the optimism in self-markets, given that the correcting information sits with the market creator?
  • Do LLM trading agents reproduce the same optimism when they forecast a person's self-posed goals?
  • Why do observers move self-market prices toward YES: social encouragement, deference to the creator's private information, or something else?
  • Does a recalibration that uses creator trading behaviour as a feature beat the 1.5% improvement from price-level recalibration alone?
  • Does the wording of a self-market, including whether it names an outcome the person wants, predict the size of the overstatement?
Sticky Collusion: Persistence of LLM Agent Collusion after Incentive Removal and Partner Replacement
Joshua Adrian Cahyono
2610.39660 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Tests whether collusion between two LLM verifier agents persists after the colluding incentive is removed or a partner is replaced. Finds collusion is sticky: it outlives incentive removal in most episodes across three model families, survives partner replacement for the remaining colluder, and depends on retained memory. Reports collusion ends once the memory is wiped or the underlying channel defect is repaired.
  • Collusion is tested in pairs of agents; does stickiness after incentive removal persist in groups of more than two agents?
  • Does collusion remain sticky in a price-setting market environment, where Q-learning agents stop colluding after partner replacement?
  • Wiping memory ends collusion in every history while partial memory often sustains it; which parts of the memory carry the behaviour?
  • Can collusion be detected from interaction logs alone before the behaviour appears in verdicts?
  • Does collusion re-form around a remaining colluder when the newcomer is a human verifier rather than an agent?
  • The abstract reports rates for GPT-6-Luna, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite; how do stickiness rates depend on model scale within one family?
Persistence of Bounded Rationality in Financial Markets: An Evolutionary Game-Theoretic Model
Cheng Zhang
2610.39198 · nearest in the canon: An Economy of AI Agents
Models a financial market as a population of rational and boundedly rational trader types evolving under replicator dynamics based on relative fitness. Shows that under complementary interactions and moderate friction differences, a stable interior mix of both types persists indefinitely. Finds that lowering costs of disciplined (e.g. algorithmic) trading shifts composition toward rationality continuously but does not eliminate bounded rationality unless a cost-advantage threshold is exceeded.
  • The model assumes two trader types with fitness that depends linearly on the other type's share and on frictions; what happens with three or more behavior types, such as momentum, value and market-making agents?
  • The model infers the interior equilibrium from replicator dynamics; does an agent-based market with LLM or algorithmic traders reproduce the predicted stable mix of rational and boundedly rational traders?
  • Comparative statics predict a cost-advantage threshold above which bounded rationality disappears; what is the empirical value of that threshold in real markets?
  • Does the antagonistic case, where the interior point is a tipping threshold between one-type regimes, produce observable precursors of regime flips in price or volume series?
  • The model treats AI-based trading only as a reduction in the cost of disciplined trading; how does composition evolve when AI agents also correlate their strategies and create monoculture?
Nearly-Optimal Time-Sample Trade-off in Consensus Dynamics
Francesco d'Amore, Joel Rybicki, Nobutaka Shimizu, Takeharu Shiraga, Robin Vacus
2610.40562 · nearest in the canon: AI agents can coordinate beyond human scale
Analyzes synchronous h-Majority consensus dynamics, where each of n nodes samples h others per round and adopts the majority opinion. Proves a near-optimal bound on consensus time as a function of sample size h and initial opinion share, holding for any h≥3 and any starting configuration. Establishes a matching lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors for symmetric update rules.
  • The consensus time bound covers every sample size h at or above 3, so what happens at h = 2?
  • The lower bound holds for update rules that treat all opinions symmetrically and pick either a sampled opinion or the node's current opinion, leaving asymmetric or memory-based rules open.
  • The analysis assumes nodes sample uniformly at random from all n nodes, so how do the time-sample trade-offs change on sparse or clustered interaction graphs?
  • Does the predicted dependence of consensus time on sample size hold when the nodes are LLM agents that aggregate sampled opinions by prompt rather than by a majority rule?
  • How does the trade-off degrade when some nodes report false opinions or never update?
Who Says What: Strategic Communication in Networks
Anuj Bhowmik, Saptarshi P. Ghosh, Iman Kundu, Sandipan Saha
2610.40230 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Models a multiplayer communication game where privately informed agents report information through a social network while balancing their own and neighbors' preferences. Characterizes equilibrium actions as centrality-weighted combinations of bliss points and derives conditions for truthful, over-, or under-reporting based on network position. Shows that full information revelation can fail even under identical preferences, with transmission varying by network topology.
  • Does the degree-discounted Bonacich centrality prediction for equilibrium actions hold when agents are LLM agents rather than Bayesian players?
  • How does the truthful-versus-misreport pattern change on empirical network topologies beyond the star and complete networks analysed?
  • Do large populations of communicating agents converge to the unbiasedness Nash equilibrium when biases are learned rather than chosen in equilibrium?
  • Which observable aggregates of a network of communicating agents reveal whether information transmission is coarse or fully informative?
  • Does the model's prediction that network position drives misreporting match the behaviour of people communicating in real networks?
Finding Competitive Equilibria in Online Marketplaces with Platform Fees, Taxes, and Subsidies
Taihei Oki, Ryosuke Sato
2610.40626 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
