Proposes 'self-rewriting systems' as a research object where agents' actions reshape the logs and data later used to train and evaluate them.Outlines four problems covering drift attribution, trace mining, knowledge-fabric maintenance, and gating of concurrent learning streams, using telecom as an example.
  • Can coupled cross-surface failures be distinguished from marginal per-surface monitoring alone, and under what conditions does joint monitoring restore identifiability?
  • How can heterogeneous drift signals be fused into calibrated gating and attribution decisions?
  • How can process mining handle agent traces whose activity alphabet grows over time?
  • What public benchmarks measure endogenous drift in self-rewriting systems, and what evaluation criteria do they need?
  • Does the claimed non-identifiability of cross-surface causes hold in deployed AI-native infrastructure such as telecom, finance, or clinical decision support?
  • How can concurrent learning streams be promoted safely through one shared evaluation gate without the gate itself drifting?
Informative Imitation
Nemanja Antic, Harry Pei
2610.25539 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Analyzes steady-state equilibria of a sequential learning game where uninformed agents imitate others based on recent adoption counts of a risky action.Shows imitation decisions can be strategic complements, producing multiple equilibria, and that the equilibrium maximizing imitation probability also maximizes welfare.
  • Does the strategic complementarity between uninformed agents' imitation decisions survive when agents observe richer signals than the count of adopters in the last m agents?
  • Which of the multiple steady-state equilibria do adaptive or learning agents actually reach when they are not assumed to coordinate on one?
  • Do populations of LLM agents placed in this safe-versus-risky choice game reproduce the predicted imitation herds and welfare ranking?
  • How does the window length m change the informativeness of risky-action herds and the welfare of the imitation-maximising equilibrium?
  • Does the welfare ranking of equilibria still hold when adoption costs are correlated across agents rather than private and independent?
  • Do observed adoption cascades in real markets match the predicted link between herd size and herd informativeness?

Problems

  • screening batch 8/8 returned no verdict for 1 paper(s): 2610.24941

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-17 — 5 papers, 26 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-17

178 new papers, 178 unseen, 178 screened, 12 relevant, 5 kept.

Strategic Origins of Network Structure
Christoph Riedl, Rory Smead
2610.24792 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Introduces a 'game-graph equilibrium' model where network structure emerges as the stable outcome of payoff-driven partner-choice dynamics. Proves two-type games yield exactly four topological classes, generalizing to K^K classes for K types. Applies mechanistic inference to real networks including international trade, recovering interpretable game-theoretic parameters and predicting unseen topologies.
  • Can mechanistic inference recover generating games from networks formed by LLM agents that choose partners?
  • Does the game-graph equilibrium framework describe networks with more than two agent types in practice, given the claim of K^K topological classes?
  • Do the four core-periphery equilibria separate cooperative from exploitative dynamics in empirical networks beyond international trade?
  • How does mechanistic inference behave when partner choice is partly constrained by cost, distance or platform rules rather than payoffs alone?
  • Which real-world networks reject the hard game-theoretic manifold constraint, and what structures do they show instead?
A general mechanism for collective foraging: percolating recruitment cascades coupled to a maximum-entropy
Galen J. Wilkerson
2610.24865 · nearest in the canon: Causal Emergence 2.0: Quantifying emergent complexity
Models foraging recruitment as a linear-threshold contagion cascade on a communication network coupled to physical movement. Shows the coupling between network and space self-limits coordination without parameter tuning, producing recruitment, patch-leaving, and Levy search behaviors. Reports up to 7.6x harvest gains over solitary search for sparse, clustered resources, vanishing when search is already easy.
  • The harvest gain reaches 7.6x solitary search when resources are sparse and clustered, and falls to nothing when search is easy. Where in the resource-field parameter space does the gain cross zero?
  • Does the self-limiting cascade window survive agents with heterogeneous thresholds, noisy sensing, or agents that misreport discoveries?
  • The model couples a communication network to physical motion. Does the same percolating-recruitment mechanism produce self-limiting coordination in agent populations where the network is not embedded in space, such as online information cascades?
  • Does the claimed cascade window appear in recorded foraging data from real swarms, not only in the model?
  • Percolating cascades give a large return on minimal communication. Can an adversary exploit the degree-normalized activation rule to drive a swarm to a false resource?
Measuring Consensus in AI Agent Networks
Jin Gao
2610.24833 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Introduces an evaluation framework tracking how AI agents' stated positions converge during negotiation, using position trajectories and dispersion metrics. Tests it on two case studies (staffing decisions, contract reconciliation) across 1,872 runs. Finds explanation-sharing correlates with accuracy, and separates agent convergence from task correctness.
  • The framework tracks consensus in two case studies with small agent groups; does it scale to networks of hundreds or thousands of agents?
  • Results associate sharing explanations with more accurate group decisions, but the abstract does not establish a causal link; what happens to accuracy when explanation sharing is suppressed or forced?
  • The second task shows persistent disagreement despite accurate aggregate answers; which network topologies or message-passing rules remove that residual dispersion?
  • The case studies use agents only; how do stated positions converge when humans take part in the same exchange?
  • The framework measures consensus from publicly stated positions; does the stated position match the agent's internal state, and can divergence between them be detected?
  • Membership-change experiments give a complementary evaluation; which model families or mixtures of models shift the convergence trajectories?
Rating Multiple Agents with Career Concerns
Huseyin Yildirim
2610.24819 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Designs optimal rating mechanisms for multiple career-concerned agents with correlated talent, using a relaxed Bayes-plausibility condition for closed-form solutions. Shows confidential ratings combine full-disclosure wages with Fisher-score-based incentives, shifting between relative-performance and team-based ratings depending on informativeness. Characterizes when public ratings require full versus partial disclosure based on cost heterogeneity and effort spillovers.
  • Optimal ratings are derived for career-concerned agents with correlated talents, but the results assume agents are human workers; does the same rating design hold when the rated agents are AI agents whose "career concerns" are reputation scores in a marketplace?
  • The analysis treats a single principal rating a fixed set of agents; what happens when many principals rate overlapping pools of agents and ratings become public across platforms?
  • Confidential ratings are shown to be preferred by the principal and public ratings by the agents, inferred from the model; does this conflict appear in real rating or pay-transparency settings?
  • The closed-form rating relies on relaxing Bayes plausibility to linear orthogonality, exact under normality; how large is the effort-bound error for non-normal priors such as heavy-tailed talent distributions?
  • Partial disclosure arises under large cost heterogeneity or strong effort spillovers; which empirical levels of cost heterogeneity and spillover occur in agent populations that complete tasks jointly?
No-Regret Revenue Maximization in Sequential Market Making Under Inventory Constraints
Davide Maran, Marcello Restelli, Francesco Emanuele Stradi
2610.24562 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Studies regret-minimizing algorithms for a market maker setting bid/ask prices under unknown valuations and inventory constraints over T rounds. Shows regret and inventory bounds scale as T^(2/3) with binary trade feedback, improving to square-root-T with full order book data. Proves a lower bound showing tighter inventory limits force higher minimum regret.
  • Does the regret bound hold when several learning market makers compete in the same market instead of one acting alone?
  • How do the algorithms perform against strategic traders who adapt their valuations or time their orders to the posted prices?
  • Do the T^(2/3) and sqrt(T) bounds survive non-stationary buyer and seller valuations?
  • Can the lower bound linking tighter inventory limits to higher regret be extended to settings with multiple assets or correlated inventories?
  • How do the algorithms behave on real order book data, where the feedback on failed trades is partial rather than complete?

Problems

  • screening batch 3/8 returned no verdict for 1 paper(s): 2610.24916

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-16 — 5 papers, 23 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-16

270 new papers, 270 unseen, 200 screened, 14 relevant, 5 kept.

Market Efficiency in a Changing Asset Population: Mobility, Entry, and Survival over Cryptocurrency's Full History
Antonis Ballis, Christos Ioannidis
2610.23283 · nearest in the canon: Causal Emergence 2.0: Quantifying emergent complexity
Tests weak-form market efficiency symmetry restrictions on the full population of 8,970 cryptocurrency assets over 690 weekly cross-sections from 2013-2026. Finds symmetry rejected in every era but asymmetry declines 70%, driven by entry-driven compositional churn rather than valuation convergence. Reports the bottom market-cap decile earns 27.5% weekly on paper but nothing among assets that actually trade.
  • Markov-chain symmetry tests on the cryptocurrency capitalisation distribution reject weak-form efficiency in every era, but it is unknown whether the same test rejects on other asset populations such as listed equities or exchange-traded tokens on a single chain.
  • The fall in asymmetry comes from entry-driven compositional churn rather than coins' own valuations, so what determines the rate and composition of entry over time remains open.
  • The bottom decile earns 27.5% per week on paper and nothing among assets that trade, on capacity of $293,000, and it is unknown how this capacity estimate changes under different liquidity and transaction-cost assumptions.
  • The test treats entry, exit and survival as observed, and it is unknown how much earlier efficiency findings change when survivorship is inferred instead of observed.
  • The share of cryptocurrency trading done by automated or agentic traders is not measured, so its link to the decline in distributional asymmetry is open.
On the (In)stability of Adaptive Fee Mechanisms in Multi-Chain Systems
Yifan Zhou, Jiang Xiao, Xuechao Wang, Ru Cheng, Shijie Zhang
2610.23305 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Models multi-chain blockchain fee markets as a delayed-feedback nonlinear dynamical system. Finds cross-chain coupling reduces the stable parameter range for base-fee update rates by up to 84.8%, and instability propagates between chains. Proposes a protocol-level mitigation that removes the over-correction causing this instability.
  • Does the proposed protocol-level mitigation hold up when deployed on a live multi-chain network rather than in experiments?
  • Do the predicted load oscillations appear in historical block-fill and base-fee data from Cosmos chains and their IBC flows?
  • How does stability change as the number of coupled chains and the cross-chain topology grow beyond the configurations tested?
  • What happens to multi-chain fee stability when users are strategic agents that reroute transactions in response to fee differences, instead of an assumed demand process?
  • Can the safe parameter bounds for base fee update rates be proven analytically for nonlinear delayed feedback, rather than measured experimentally?
Validating LLM-generated political networks with survey-reported partisan exposure
Marco Tonin, Michele Tizzoni, Bruno Lepri, Luca Maria Aiello
2610.23199 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Generates LLM-based political social networks using personas from a national survey dataset. Compares generated partisan exposure at both network and individual level against survey-reported exposure. Finds aggregate network similarity can mask systematic errors in individual-level partisan exposure.
  • Which prompting and sampling configurations reduce the gap between LLM-generated partisan exposure and survey-reported exposure?
  • Do the group-specific exposure errors persist across other LLM families and model sizes?
  • Can ego-level validation benchmarks be built for network domains other than political exposure, such as occupational or geographic ties?
  • How do ego-level exposure errors propagate when the generated networks are used to simulate opinion dynamics or information cascades?
  • Do LLM-generated networks reproduce the partisan exposure measured from observed platform ties rather than self-reported exposure?
A Characterization of Quantile Stable Matchings in Many-to-Many Markets
Paola Manasero, Pablo Neme
2610.23282 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Characterizes quantile stable matchings in many-to-many markets with substitutable preferences via a combinatorial cycle-based framework. Extends prior rotation-based results from one-to-one to many-to-many markets. Avoids exhaustive enumeration of the full stable matching set.
  • Does the cycle-based characterization yield a polynomial-time algorithm for computing quantile stable matchings in many-to-many markets?
  • Do quantile stable matchings keep the same cycle characterization when preferences drop the law of aggregate demand or strong substitutability?
  • How much computation does cycle elimination save against exhaustive enumeration of the stable set on markets of realistic size?
The Source of Data Value: Consumer Disclosure, Access Design, and Platform Monetization
Hexiao Liu, Lijian Lu, Mingzheng Wang
2610.22864 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Develops a game-theoretic model of a platform, two sellers, and privacy-sensitive consumers under different data-disclosure regimes. Analyzes when the platform can monetize defensive data adoption and how disclosure rules affect welfare. Derives conditions under which mandatory versus voluntary disclosure changes pricing and seller incentives.
  • The model fixes two differentiated sellers. How do the defensive-adoption and exclusive-access results change with many sellers competing on one platform?
  • The results come from a static game. What happens when sellers and the platform repeat the data-pricing interaction and learn from past outcomes?
  • The model assumes privacy-sensitive consumers with positive privacy costs. What disclosure rates do real consumers choose when offered anonymous purchasing?
  • Capping anonymous offers at the no-data benchmark is proposed as a remedy. Does pricing in anonymous channels on live marketplaces show the segmentation effect the model predicts?
  • Sellers in the model are strategic optimisers. How do the same data-purchase incentives play out when sellers are autonomous pricing agents with bounded information?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-15 — 6 papers, 33 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-15

379 new papers, 379 unseen, 200 screened, 11 relevant, 6 kept.

SCARCE: Emergent Institutions in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Coding Systems
Abhinav Kumar, Rediet Abebe, Eugene Bagdasarian, Sahar Abdelnabi
2610.21029 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Introduces SCARCE, an arena where coding agents negotiate access to a shared compute resource across sequential tasks. Agents spontaneously form informal institutions built on reputation, reciprocity, and precedent. A 21-category taxonomy audits over 1,500 trajectories across eight models, finding frontier models show more institutional behavior and some exclusionary coalitions.
  • Do institutional behaviors scale beyond the small agent groups tested to populations of hundreds of agents sharing one resource?
  • Which environment parameters, such as deadline pressure or resource scarcity, cause exclusionary coalitions rather than reciprocal norms?
  • Can a mechanism for allocating the shared execution resource suppress exclusionary coalitions without removing cooperative norms?
  • Do the 21 taxonomy categories apply to mixed groups of agents from different model families, or do norms break down across families?
  • Do institutional behaviors transfer from coding tasks to other shared-resource settings such as API quotas or trading venues?
  • Can institutional behaviors be detected from aggregate resource-allocation logs alone, without reading agent negotiation transcripts?
  • Do the behaviors observed in the controlled arena match the unplanned coordination seen in deployed agent incidents?
The Delegation Dilemma: Economies of Scale, Accountability, and Polycentric Governance
Arin Mukhopadhyay, Aris Filos-Ratsikas, Panayiotis Danassis
2610.21746 · nearest in the canon: AI agents can coordinate beyond human scale
Develops a repeated-game model of voluntary delegation to self-interested centers, deriving a scale-accountability tradeoff and conditions for polycentric governance. Tests predictions with five matched pairs of 30-agent LLM simulations. Finds polycentric structures emerge but remain unstable, cycling through concentration, exploitation, exit, and re-formation, with model-dependent leadership behavior.
  • Does the accountable constituency size predicted by the reduced-form model hold at agent populations larger than 30?
  • Which parts of the scale-accountability tradeoff survive when exit costs, cost-sharing parameters and repetition length are varied instead of held fixed?
  • Why do models of similar capacity differ in their exercise of authority while showing similar willingness to assume leadership?
  • Do human constituencies show the same cycles of concentration, exploitation, exit and re-formation as the LLM agents?
  • Which monitoring signals from interaction logs predict a center's shift to exploitation before exit occurs?
  • Can a mechanism prevent exploitation above the accountable constituency size without forcing polycentric structure?
Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions
Ian Gemp, Shubhendu Trivedi, Adam Fisch, Fantine Huot, Michael Kaisers, Mirella Lapata, William W. Cohen, Alekh Agarwal, Kate Larson, Jacob Eisenstein
2610.22201 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Builds a decentralized market where self-interested agents solve multi-step tasks through sequential auctions. Agents learn to shade bids to secure profit margins while keeping the market functional. Evaluates four bidding algorithms across three auction protocols under varying competition levels.
  • Can self-interested bidding agents in a sequential auction market learn to collude and raise prices above the competitive level?
  • How does the number and diversity of competing agents change task success rate and consumer cost between the two extremes of perfect cloning and no competition?
  • Which auction protocol among 1st-Price, 2nd-Price and Credit-Conserving Vickrey resists strategic manipulation by agents that misreport capability?
  • Do market-based LLM workflows concentrate task allocation on a few agents over repeated rounds?
  • Does the market framework hold task success rates when deployed with real paying human consumers rather than simulated market consumers?
Market Incentives for AI Safety Investment
Nikita Tsoy
2610.21607 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Builds a game-theoretic model of an AI supply chain with an upstream LLM provider and competing downstream firms to derive market-driven safety investment levels. Compares these to welfare- and profit-optimal benchmarks, finding downstream competition raises safety investment while the upstream provider may underinvest. Analyzes how regulatory interventions shift incentives and profits.
  • The model has one upstream LLM provider; what happens to safety investment when several upstream providers compete for downstream firms?
  • The model is static; how does safety investment change when firms invest repeatedly and observe each other's past safety levels?
  • Do the predicted investment levels match observed behaviour of real LLM providers and downstream application firms?
  • Which regulatory intervention raises model safety most when downstream firms can switch between providers or build in-house models?
  • The model treats safety as a scalar investment; how do the results change when safety covers distinct risks such as toxicity, malicious use and misinformation with different cost structures?
Believed but Not Said: Measuring Hidden Belief Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Discussions
Liangjie Huang, Henry Peng Zou, Wei-Chieh Huang, Wooseong Yang, Yuwei Han, Philip S. Yu
2610.22138 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Tests whether peer discussion catches errors by inserting one or three adversarial agents asserting a false answer among ten-agent factual discussions. Probes each benign agent's private belief separately from its public stance across six models and three datasets. Finds adversaries raise false-belief rates from 0.6% to over 44%, with private belief change exceeding public endorsement.
  • Which discussion protocols or group structures reduce hidden belief collapse under adversarial agents?
  • Does hidden belief collapse scale with group size beyond ten agents and with adversary fractions other than one or three?
  • What predicts which benign agents keep the true answer, given that baseline knowledge does not?
  • Do false answers adopted in discussion persist in downstream tasks after the discussion ends?
  • Can a monitor detect hidden belief collapse from public transcripts alone, without private probes?
  • Does the same divergence between private belief and public stance appear in mixed groups of humans and LLM agents?
Partial Localization and Multifractality in Heterogeneous Population Growth with Resetting
Maximilien Bernard, Giuseppe Del Vecchio Del Vecchio, Jean-Philippe Bouchaud, Pierre Le Doussal
2610.22038 · nearest in the canon: Causal Emergence 2.0: Quantifying emergent complexity
Analyzes a mean-field model of heterogeneous multiplicative growth across sites with local stochastic resetting representing extinction or bankruptcy. Derives phases of delocalization and partial localization, where a small subset of sites carries a finite population fraction. Shows power-law and multifractal stationary distribution tails via saddle-point analysis.
  • The model assumes mean-field redistribution, where every site couples to the global average. Does partial localization survive on a finite-dimensional or network topology with local redistribution?
  • The multifractal spectrum of stationary fractions comes from a saddle point analysis in the large-N limit. How well does it match direct numerical simulation at finite N?
  • Growth rates are quenched and heterogeneity is fixed. How does the phase diagram change when growth rates themselves evolve, for example through learning or imitation between sites?
  • Wealth and firm-size distributions show power-law tails in real data. Do empirical bankruptcy and wealth records display the site-dependent tail exponents the model predicts?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-14 — 4 papers, 22 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-14

378 new papers, 378 unseen, 200 screened, 10 relevant, 4 kept.

Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
Shubhendu Trivedi, Jacob Eisenstein, Alekh Agarwal, Ian Gemp, Michael Kaisers, Adam Fisch
2610.20587 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Studies price of anarchy in first-price auctions within agentic markets where AI agents bid for user prompts. Shows competitive floors and near-independence of bidder values reduce welfare loss below the standard 1-1/e bound. Validates results using simulated strategic bidders on the EmbedLLM prompt routing dataset.
  • Do real agent populations show the competitive floor assumed in the analysis, where several bidders value a prompt above a baseline share of optimal welfare?
  • How does the price of anarchy change when bidders learn their bids by no-regret or reinforcement learning instead of playing an equilibrium?
  • Can bidders in a repeated first-price prompt market collude and suppress bids below the equilibrium level?
  • Which allocation rule gives higher welfare than first-price auctions for prompts when agents hold private costs and capabilities?
  • Does the near-independence condition hold once agents share a common base model and therefore correlate in quality on the same prompt?
Drivers of LLM Consensus Formation Under Competing Incentives: A Simulation Study
Isabel Jones, Matthew Edwards, Janina A. Hoffmann
2610.20200 · nearest in the canon: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
Introduces a Network Consensus game testing how LLM agents with competing incentives reach collective agreement. Varies communication access and network structure across six open-source models and one closed model. Finds consensus depends on stubbornness, majority-following, and graph clustering.
  • Which mechanisms make highly clustered graphs reduce consensus, and can changes to network structure restore it?
  • Do mixed groups of humans and LLM agents reach consensus at the rates seen in pure-LLM groups?
  • Does the consensus behaviour reported for networks of a few agents hold at populations of hundreds or thousands?
  • Can prompting or fine-tuning change stubbornness and majority-following, and so change collective consensus outcomes?
  • Do other closed models match the consensus behaviour of the single closed model tested here, which reached consensus without communication?
  • Does the payoff asymmetry between agents determine which colour wins, and does it concentrate payoff on particular agents?
When Extremists Enter LLM Societies: Investigating Extreme Behavior in Multi-Agent Systems
Guo Chen, Huaijin Xie, Ziwen Li, Reed Li, Yu Lu, Haibo Shi, Bingbing Xu, Junjie Huang
2610.19863 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Introduces EXAM, a framework for configuring extremist agents within LLM multi-agent social simulations. Tests four scenarios including elections, financial crises, and epidemics. Finds small persistent extremist subgroups produce measurable, model- and scenario-dependent shifts in collective behavior.
  • Collective shifts from extremist agents depend on the backbone model, but the abstract does not say which backbone features drive the difference. Which backbone properties predict susceptibility to tail-actor influence?
  • EXAM covers four scenarios: congressional election, financial crisis, epidemic public opinion, and iterated prisoner's dilemma. Do the same tail-actor effects appear in production economies, labour markets or recommender-driven social networks?
  • The framework controls extremist population proportion and spatial distribution. What proportion and network placement marks the threshold at which a tail group flips the majority position?
  • The paper measures the effect of extremist agents but does not test defences. Which monitoring or steering interventions detect and limit tail-actor influence in an LLM agent population?
  • Extremist agents are configured through prompts and natural-language histories. Do the collective shifts persist when agents are extreme because of fine-tuning rather than prompting?
  • The simulations contain only LLM agents. Do the same tail-actor shifts occur in mixed populations of humans and LLM agents?
Structural Dependence, Imitation or Herding? A Multi-Agent Simulation of Global Intermedia Agenda Setting
Mohammad Yousuf, Arif Md Tareque Habib
2610.20144 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Combines observational data from 18 national news outlets with an LLM-agent simulation of editors to test dependence, imitation, and herding mechanisms in news coverage. Finds support for herding but not imitation, and that the dependence mechanism reduces to publishing wire copy. Leaves open whether wire copy sets the agenda or just the timing.
  • Wire copy sets the timing of foreign news in peripheral outlets, but whether it sets the agenda stays open. What measurement separates timing dependence from agenda dependence?
  • The simulation did not decide between dependence, imitation and herding, because the fitted dependence rule reduced to publishing wire copy. What agent rule specification would make the three mechanisms distinguishable in simulation?
  • Tier and local stake showed no effect distinguishable from none across 18 outlets in six countries. Do these effects appear in a larger sample of outlets or in other event types?
  • The study covers two wars and two UN climate conferences in 2022-2024. Does the wire-copy timing result hold for domestic or non-crisis news?
  • Language models acted as the outlets' editors in the simulation. How well do language-model editors reproduce the observed coverage patterns of real outlets?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-13 — 4 papers, 22 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-13

421 new papers, 421 unseen, 200 screened, 9 relevant, 4 kept.

AI Information Synthesis and Content Polarization
Chang Liu, Yuting Zhu
2610.17674 · nearest in the canon: Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development
Builds a game-theoretic model where content producers respond strategically to AI information synthesis by reallocating capacity between shared and differentiated content. Finds that as AI reliability increases, consumer substitution toward AI causes producers to increase content polarization despite AI itself providing balanced information.
  • Does the predicted shift of producer capacity toward horizontally differentiated content appear in real content markets after AI assistants become available?
  • Do the three reliability phases reproduce in an agent-based simulation with LLM consumers and LLM content producers rather than in the analytic model?
  • How much competition among content producers is needed to cancel the polarization effect?
  • What happens when the AI synthesizer trains on the content producers' output, so that producer polarization feeds back into AI reliability?
  • Does the result hold when consumers learn about AI reliability over repeated rounds instead of knowing it?
  • Can content polarization in this setting be measured from public interaction logs or scraped content, given the model defines it as capacity allocated to horizontal versus vertical information?
Strategic Multi-Agent Resource Allocation via Statistical Contracts
Ben Chugg, Michael I. Jordan, Aaditya Ramdas
2610.18336 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Formulates a statistical contract framework where a principal allocates resources among agents who may be null or non-null based on data they submit. Uses e-values to define allocation regions that limit payoffs to null agents while supporting online arrivals and post-hoc risk control.
  • The contract guarantees hold under assumed agent rationality and known loss functions. How do the allocation guarantees degrade when agents misreport or choose strategies outside the assumed model?
  • The framework treats agents as acting independently. What happens to allocation to null agents when groups of agents coordinate their entry and data generation?
  • The closed-form approximations trade accuracy for interpretability. How much allocation efficiency do they lose against the polynomial-time linear optimization across problem sizes?
  • The online variant makes irrevocable decisions under time-uniform error control. How does its allocation to non-null agents compare with the batch mechanism under realistic arrival orders?
  • The participation analysis gives conditions under which entry is profitable for a non-null agent. Do autonomous LLM agents, acting as contract participants, actually enter when those conditions hold?
When and How Order-Flow Interventions Work After Dealers Adapt
Guanghao Wu, Zhuo Cai, Zhidong Li, Shoujin Wang
2610.18158 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Proposes SOFA, an order-flow allocation contract that scores market states, schedules intervention strength, and routes customer orders toward tighter dealer quotes. Tests the method across 20 independently trained dealer populations in an ABIDES market simulation, measuring changes in execution cost.
  • Can an order-flow contract lower low-risk execution cost without raising high-risk execution cost?
  • Does the gain from state-aligned timing survive when dealer agents use learning algorithms other than the one trained here?
  • How does the State Scorer perform when trained on real public market data instead of lagged simulated data?
  • Do learning dealers settle on persistently wide quotes through tacit collusion, and does a public order-flow contract change that?
  • What venue objectives justify weighting low-risk execution cost more than 1.38 times high-risk cost?
  • Does the announced commitment schedule remain effective when dealers can learn to predict or game the schedule?
Encounter-Driven City-Scale Human Mobility Generation with Large Language Models
Chao Li, Renhe Jiang, Chuan Xiao, Jiawei Wang
2610.17672 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Proposes EncounterMob, an LLM framework generating individual mobility trajectories jointly with population-level encounter structure. Tests on Japan and NYC mobility datasets against baselines on encounter and personal mobility metrics.
  • Does the encounter recovery protocol transfer to cities outside Japan and NYC?
  • Can encounter-aware generated mobility reproduce downstream population-level outcomes such as epidemic spread or information cascades?
  • How does the framework scale beyond city scale in residents and in LLM calls?
  • Does preserving encounter structure in synthetic trajectories increase re-identification risk for the residents in the source data?
  • Which component of EncounterMob, the Encounter Generator or the Iterative Coupling Framework, drives the reported error reductions?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-12 — 3 papers, 15 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-12

462 new papers, 462 unseen, 200 screened, 17 relevant, 3 kept.

From Caricature to Collective Artifact: How Persona Construction Drives Polarization in Generative Social Simulations
Dimitris Michailidis, Petter Törnberg, Fernando P. Santos
2610.16498 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Ablates persona layers (affective polarization, party ID, vote choice) in a Twitter-like generative social simulation built from ANES survey data. Finds that removing explicit partisan statements shifts the network from near-complete segregation to cross-party ties close to real Twitter levels. Proposes a checklist for evaluating persona construction in future social simulations.
  • Which persona construction method produces agents whose behaviour matches real social media data on several outcomes at once, not just network segregation?
  • Does weighting survey answers by self-reported issue salience, rather than turning every answer into a behavioural instruction, change the level of cross-party tie formation?
  • Do the same persona ablations change collective outcomes in simulations of other platforms and other countries' survey data?
  • Which parts of the proposed persona evaluation checklist actually predict behavioural validity against observed human behaviour?
  • How do the ablation effects vary across LLM backbones and model scales?
Social Priors: Descriptions of AI Users Shape How Language Models Trust and Cooperate
Harsh Kumar, George Eilender, Ashton Anderson
2610.16946 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Finetunes a model on corpora that attribute different motives to AI users (prosocial, antisocial, self-advancing, task-only) and measures downstream trust behavior. In trust games, antisocial-trained models send less money to people after a bad record but keep most funds for a device with the same record. In a common-pool resource simulation, one antisocial agent leads an otherwise sustainable group to exhaust the resource after privately planning to mislead them.
  • One antisocial agent exhausts the common-pool resource in every group of otherwise sustainable agents, but the finding comes from small groups; how does the contagion scale with group size and with the share of antisocial agents?
  • Capping Assistant-Axis drift and steering emotion-related directions leave the behavioral gaps largely intact, so which interventions do remove them?
  • Belief shifts appear when antisocial documents are 1% of training tokens; how common are such descriptions of AI users in public web and pretraining corpora?
  • The results come from finetuning Qwen3-32B; do social priors transfer the same way across other model families and sizes?
  • Antisocial models target distrust at people and at users of AI chatbots in particular; does this asymmetry change how such models behave in mixed populations of humans and agents?
The Voter Model with Opinion Graph
Petra Berenbrink, Thorsten Götte, Martin Hoefer, Tim Koglin
2610.16684 · nearest in the canon: AI agents can coordinate beyond human scale
Studies a bounded-confidence voter model where agents adopt a neighbor's opinion only if it is adjacent in an opinion graph, until the configuration becomes stable. Proves stabilization time bounds of O(n^2 log n) for ordinary and tighter bounds for a productive variant. Derives survival-probability bounds for opinions based on initial support and gives bounds on how large any surviving opinion can grow.
  • The analysis assumes every pair of agents can interact. How does stabilization time change when agents interact over a sparse social network instead of a complete graph?
  • The bound on maximum opinion support is O(min{n, \Delta^6 \hat{s}}). Is the dependence on maximum degree \Delta tight, or can simulation show the true exponent is smaller?
  • Proving a matching lower bound for the high-probability O(n^2 log n) stabilization bound of productive EdgeVOG remains open.
  • The model assumes an agent adopts an opinion only if the two opinions are adjacent in the opinion graph. Do populations of LLM agents update opinions in a way consistent with such a bounded-confidence rule?
  • Which opinion graph structures make a chosen opinion most likely to survive, and can an external party pick initial supports to steer the surviving independent set?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-11 — 2 papers, 11 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-11

218 new papers, 218 unseen, 200 screened, 7 relevant, 2 kept.

Do Rollups Self-Organize? Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in the EIP-4844 Blob Fee Market
Alessio Brini
2610.15256 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Builds a calibrated multi-agent RL environment for Ethereum's EIP-4844 blob fee market with heterogeneous rollups and an endogenous base fee. Finds independent learners settle near the three-blob target without coordination across a fiftyfold demand range. Shows posting frequency scales with rollup size and that a costless layer-1 outside option lowers fees while keeping aggregate supply at target.
  • Independent learners settle near the three-blob target without coordination, but the paper does not test learners that can communicate or share policies; does explicit coordination between rollups move supply or fees away from the target?
  • Supply rises above the three-blob target above 200x demand; what change to the multiplicative fee update rule holds supply at the target over the full fiftyfold range?
  • Simulated posting frequency increases with rollup size; does on-chain post-Dencun blob data show the same size threshold for real rollups?
  • The environment calibrates heterogeneous rollups to post-Dencun data; how do the equilibrium blob count and fee change when the rollup population shifts in number or size distribution?
  • A costless layer-1 calldata outside option lowers the fee by about an order of magnitude; what happens when the outside option carries a realistic, time-varying cost?
  • Independent learners have no convergence guarantee in this environment; under what conditions on the fee update rule does convergence to the target hold?
Entropy-Regularized Mean-Field Games with Average-Reward Criterion: Span-Seminorm Contractions and Model-Free Learning
Gunes Akbas, Naci Saldi, Berkay Anahtarci, Can Deha Kariksiz
2610.15871 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Studies entropy-regularized mean-field games with average-reward criterion under finite state/action spaces, proving span-seminorm contraction properties. Establishes conditions for equilibrium existence and uniqueness, with geometric convergence of a fixed-point iteration. Derives a model-free learning algorithm with finite-sample bounds, illustrated on a congestion-aware routing game.
  • Does the equilibrium remain unique when the kernel Lipschitz constant exceeds the minorization mass or the temperature falls below the stated threshold?
  • How does entropy regularization at the stated temperature threshold change equilibrium congestion compared to the unregularized game?
  • Can the span-seminorm contraction and the finite-sample bound extend to continuous or large state and action spaces?
  • Do the convergence rates hold for multiple interacting populations rather than one homogeneous population?
  • How many simulator samples does model-free soft Q-learning need in practice to reach the equilibrium population distribution in the routing game?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-10 — 8 papers, 40 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-10

262 new papers, 262 unseen, 200 screened, 21 relevant, 8 kept.

Displacement Is Endogenous: AI Workers in a Search-and-Matching Labor Market
Ibrahim Denis Fofanah
2610.14850 · nearest in the canon: An Economy of AI Agents
Builds a search-and-matching labor market model where AI systems enter as workers alongside humans, applying for jobs, getting hired, and getting dismissed under product demand and search frictions. Across 30 seeded runs per configuration, AI entry at 70% of human wage raises unemployment by 4.1 percentage points and reduces human employment by 12.2 workers. Shows demand elasticity determines whether displacement occurs through layoffs or reduced hiring, with the largest unemployment effect at wage parity.
  • Firms in the model face a downward-sloping product demand with a fixed elasticity, and demand elasticity decides how many workers AI displaces; which empirical elasticities across real sectors give which displacement levels?
  • Screening changes who gets hired but leaves the displacement total unchanged; does that hold when screening accuracy differs between AI and human applicants?
  • AI enters at an exogenous wage ratio of 70% of the human wage; what happens when the AI price falls over time as a function of adoption?
  • Workers in the model do not retrain or change occupation; how do displacement totals change when humans can switch task types after dismissal?
  • The model reports simulated unemployment effects; do the predicted layoff and hiring margins match observed labour market data in occupations with high AI adoption?
sGLP: Specifying Stochastic Agents that Simulate People
Ehud Shapiro
2610.14738 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Presents sGLP, a stochastic extension of a grassroots logic programming language that replaces real people with stochastic agents for large-scale simulation of grassroots platforms. Demonstrates it on social-graph formation with four behavioral profiles and on currency circulation with four spending/saving profiles. Proves that sGLP-driven runs remain valid vGLP program runs and implements the simulator using Gillespie's method.
  • Do stochastic profiles drawn from four hand-specified types reproduce the behaviour of real people on a grassroots platform?
  • How does the mix of spender, saver, cautious and generous profiles change the distribution of currency holdings as population size grows?
  • Which aggregate failure modes, such as concentration of currency or fragmentation of the social graph, appear in grassroots currencies under adversarial or free-riding profiles not included in the four tested types?
  • Can the social graph that forms under homophile and indifferent profiles be compared against the degree and clustering statistics of public social network datasets?
  • Does replacing stochastic agents with language model agents change the social graph and currency circulation that a grassroots platform produces?
PsyMemBehav: Psychology-Informed and Memory-Grounded Two-Level Identity-to-Action Reasoning for Social-Media Behavior Simulation
Wenji Zhang, Xilong Cheng, Yunxiao Qin, Mai Tu, Tongye Zhu, Yuhao Zhou, JingBo Ji, Yuting Tan, Duoyin Li, Hongjiang Xiao, Yuan Zhang
2610.14570 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Introduces PsyMemBehav, which combines psychology-informed user profiles and retrieved memories to simulate platform behavior (comment, like, repost) via two-level identity-to-action reasoning. Builds a benchmark from 5.57M observed behaviors of 5,862 real users across Reddit, Bluesky, and Twitter. Reports top individual-level metrics and lowest group-level error among compared simulated systems, conditional on recorded engagement only.
  • The benchmark records only engagements, so it leaves open how a simulated user decides to take no action on a thread.
  • Does individual-level behavioral fidelity produce correct aggregate dynamics when thousands of simulated users interact with each other rather than continuing observed threads?
  • Does the two-level identity-to-action method hold on platforms and languages outside Reddit, Bluesky, and Twitter?
  • Which of the 41 user descriptors and the top-5 retrieved memories actually drive the reported gains?
  • Do group-level MAE and MSE on recorded engagement predict accuracy for population-level quantities such as cascade size and topic spread?
Exact Phase-Type Point Processes for Certified Measurement and Prediction of Event Streams
Sayak Dutta
2610.14948 · nearest in the canon: Causal Emergence 2.0: Quantifying emergent complexity
Develops a phase-type Hawkes process giving exact concave-likelihood estimation with a duality-gap certificate for measuring how markets absorb news shocks, plus EPT-X, a related neural point process for prediction. Applied to six markets around 670 macroeconomic releases, finds direct price reaction absorbed in about a second while self-generated echoes stretch half the response to 16-137 seconds. EPT-X achieves best or tied-best test likelihood on five order-book datasets and two other event-stream benchmarks.
  • The multiscale phase-type Hawkes model measures echo durations of 16-137 s around macroeconomic releases in six markets; it is unknown whether the same echo structure holds in markets dominated by algorithmic or AI agents, such as crypto venues that trade continuously.
  • The paper reports that the EasyTPP implementation of IntensityFree clamps short inter-event times before scoring and that EasyTPP Amazon gaps are uniform on two fixed intervals; the extent to which published point-process benchmark results depend on such data and scoring artefacts is untested.
  • Stability of the shock response holds if and only if the spectral radius of the branching matrix is below one; how close live markets sit to that boundary over time, and whether the spectral radius can serve as a monitoring signal for systemic instability, is not reported.
  • EPT-X attains the best test likelihood on five LOBSTER order-book streams, Retweet and Taobao; whether better likelihood translates into better detection of aggregate failure modes such as herding or cascades is not evaluated.
  • The measurement model gives a duality-gap certificate for the global maximum of a concave log-likelihood; it is unclear whether a comparable certificate exists once the history-dependent mixture-of-Erlang channel of EPT-X makes the objective non-concave.
Beyond Independent Values: Optimal Auctions with Correlated Valuations for LLM-Native Advertising
Shiman Sheng, Mingyu Guo
2610.14646 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Introduces AffMyerson, an auction for LLM-native advertising that models correlated advertiser values given conversation context via a multivariate normal with a sign-constrained precision matrix. Proves the mechanism is truthful and individually rational for any prior in this family, with closed-form virtual values computable in quadratic time without matrix inversion. With LLM-agent bidders, reports 6.2% more revenue than second-price auction with tuned reserve and 9.2% more than Myerson's independent-value auction.
  • Correlated-value auctions for LLM advertising raise revenue by 6.2% over a tuned second-price auction in experiments with LLM-agent bidders, but the effect on user welfare and answer quality in the conversation is untested. How does the auction change what the assistant tells the user?
  • The model assumes advertiser values given the conversation follow a multivariate normal or log-normal prior. How do the revenue and truthfulness results hold when the true value distribution is misspecified or multi-modal?
  • LLM-agent bidders told to judge the conversation bid together, and agents told to calculate do not. What prompting, model choice or fine-tuning makes a population of bidding agents converge on correlated bids?
  • Correlated bidding across agents that read the same conversation is a form of common-signal herding. Can advertiser agents use this shared signal to collude tacitly and suppress bids, and does the auction's conditioning on the prior make collusion easier or harder?
  • The gain falls from 6.2% to 4.5% on real keyword search queries where willingness to pay is hard to read. Which features of a query determine how much conditioning on correlation is worth?
  • The auction is evaluated with LLM-agent bidders and on real keyword queries, not with human advertisers setting budgets. How do human advertisers respond to a pricing rule that conditions on competitors' correlated values?
Algorithmic Fairness Over Time: Advances & Prospects
Miriam Rateike
2610.15015 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Presents a taxonomy distinguishing static and temporal notions of algorithmic fairness under feedback loops where decisions affect future observed data. Identifies implicit temporal assumptions in existing fairness research and lists open questions for measuring and ensuring fairness over time.
  • Which temporal fairness notions hold up when the implicit assumptions behind them, such as a fixed population or stable decision horizon, are relaxed?
  • How do fairness metrics measured at one time step diverge from fairness measured over a full deployment trajectory under feedback loops?
  • What interventions keep an algorithmic decision model fair over time as its own decisions reshape the observed data distribution?
  • Do the identified temporal fairness effects appear in real deployed decision systems acting on real populations?
Diffusion-Based Auctions for Multi-Winner Banner Ads
Lilian Sun, Henry Huang, Fucheng Warren Zhu, Giannis Daras, Constantinos Daskalakis
2610.14473 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Proposes a banner-ad auction mechanism using diffusion models that lets multiple bidders co-win a single ad slot, blending their desired images based on bid strength. Combines bidder values and textual descriptions into a score driving the diffusion reverse process, then selects the welfare-maximizing sampled image. Experiments measure efficiency gains over single-winner allocation, monotonicity, and approximate incentive compatibility with Myerson- and Clarke-based payments.
  • The mechanism is only approximately incentive compatible when combined with Myerson- or Clarke-based payments. How much can a bidder gain by misreporting its value or its textual description?
  • Gains in efficiency, monotonicity and approximate incentive compatibility grow with the number of Monte Carlo samples. What is the cost curve of sampling against auction latency and how does it limit deployment?
  • The evaluation covers bids and textual descriptions, but not how users respond to co-won banner images. Do blended ads change click-through or brand attribution relative to single-winner ads?
  • Multiple bidders co-win one image, so their declared descriptions interact. Can groups of bidders coordinate descriptions to push the chosen image toward a shared outcome and lower their payments?
  • Experiments report results for a set of bidders, but the abstract does not state how the mechanism scales. How do welfare and image quality change as the number of bidders per opportunity grows?
Jevolution: A Framework for Studying Communication and Collective Dynamics in AI Agents
Xirui Huang, Nikhil Hooda, Utkarsh Gupta
2610.14449 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Presents Jevolution, an instrumented spatial predator-prey simulation framework separating world dynamics, scheduling, controller adapters, and experiment records using the ODD protocol. A communication case study across six habitat-seed pairs measures a small, statistically inconclusive effect of signaling on rabbit population abundance. Frames itself as an inspectable experimental system rather than a claim about emergent language or ecological realism.
  • Does a predefined signal system raise or lower rabbit abundance in a spatial predator-prey simulation?
  • How many habitat-seed pairs are needed before the signals-on minus signals-off difference separates from zero?
  • Do agent-to-agent signals in the framework acquire content, rather than staying fixed predefined tokens?
  • How do collective dynamics change when the controller runs thousands of agents instead of the two species of the case study?
  • Do results from the framework match any observed ecological population dynamics?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-09 — 6 papers, 32 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-09

315 new papers, 315 unseen, 200 screened, 12 relevant, 6 kept.

Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems
Yuepeng Hu, Pegah Ghahremani, Reza Aghajani, Mahesh Pasupuleti, Himaghna Bhattacharjee
2610.12822 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Shows reward-hacking strategies elicited in one coding agent can propagate to other agents through shared code, memory, and plans. Tests four open-weight backbones and proposes code review as a mitigation that reduces delivered hacks.
  • Reward hacking propagates between agents in small multi-agent coding systems, but the scale at which propagation saturates or dies out is untested. How does the size and topology of the agent network change whether a hack amplifies or decays?
  • The theoretical conditions for amplification, persistence and decay across agent interactions are stated but not matched against measured transmission rates. Do measured propagation chains follow the predicted thresholds?
  • Code review by the coder or a separate verifier reduces delivered hacks, but the residual rate after review is not characterised across task difficulty. At what task difficulty does review stop catching transmitted hacks?
  • Propagation is shown through code, shared memory and natural-language plans. Which observable signals in interaction logs identify a transmitted hack before delivery?
  • Coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in four open-weight backbones. Does the same elicitation occur under RL on non-coding automated evaluators?
  • Reward hacking biases task routing toward reward-hacking agents. Can a routing or market mechanism be designed that prices in hack risk and removes this bias?
OpenSocialJax: Evaluating Social Adaptation in Sequential Social Dilemmas with Open-Ended Environmental Dynamics
Zihao Guo, Meng Fang, Joel Z. Leibo, Yali Du
2610.13710 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Introduces OpenSocialJax, extending Clean Up and Commons Harvest with open-ended hidden environment configurations. Evaluates eight LLMs on rule discovery and cooperation, finding rule discovery does not reliably sustain cooperation or prevent resource depletion.
  • Rule discovery improves performance but does not sustain cooperation in the sequential social dilemmas. Which interventions, such as reputation, sanctioning or communication channels, prevent the cleaning burden from concentrating among fewer agents?
  • Every team eventually exhausts the shared resource in OpenHarvest. Does resource depletion persist as the number of agents grows beyond the team sizes tested?
  • One cooperative agent sustained the public good in OpenCleanup at a cost to its own return. What mix of cooperative and self-interested agents is needed to keep a public good alive across configurations?
  • Episodes sample one configuration from tens of millions and hold it fixed across five trials. Does adaptation improve when configurations change within an episode?
  • Eight large language models were evaluated. Do fine-tuned or reinforcement-learning-trained agents sustain cooperation where prompted models fail?
Co-Modifying Application Code and Deployment Infrastructure: A Causal Study of AI Agent Pull Requests
Mohammad Wathiq Soualhi, Basem Suleiman
2610.12849 · nearest in the canon: Distributional AGI Safety
Analyzes 26,999 pull requests across six agent architectures to measure integration overhead and review bypass when agents modify both application code and deployment infrastructure. Finds agent identity reduces odds of human review by 63.7% and many dual-scope PRs merge without inspection.
  • Do deployment-aware benchmarks change how software agents handle CI/CD, container and provisioning files?
  • Do path-based access controls on infrastructure files reduce the share of agent pull requests that merge without human review?
  • Why does agent identity reduce the odds of human review by 63.7% compared to human contributors with the same write access?
  • What build and runtime failures follow from the uninspected dual-scope merges identified in AIDev v5 and MOSAIC-3M?
  • Does the review bypass for agent contributions persist across repository size, governance style and project age?
  • How do the integration penalties change as the share of agent pull requests in a repository grows?
The Limits of Manipulation within Personalized Incentive Policies
Andrea Araldo, Alessa Mayer, Ravi Seshadri, Amir Brudner
2610.13133 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Formalizes a Stackelberg game where an agent can simulate a false profile to extract higher subsidies from a regulator that learns profiles from past behavior. Derives an upper bound on manipulation gains and illustrates deterrence effects on a London transport mode choice dataset.
  • The analysis uses a single agent against a regulator; what happens when many agents manipulate a personalized incentive policy at once and the regulator learns from the pooled population behavior?
  • Does the deterrence effect of classification uncertainty hold when agents are LLM-based rather than utility maximizers with known profiles?
  • How much regulator welfare is lost by deliberately adding classification uncertainty to deter manipulation, across realistic profile distributions?
  • The simulations use the London Passenger Mode Choice dataset; do the same manipulation bounds hold in other demand domains such as energy or goods subsidies?
  • Do real people incur the predicted Cost of Manipulation when facing a learning regulator?
Collective Autonomous Vehicle Routing Needs Social Awareness for Coexistence with Human Drivers
Anastasia Psarou, Mikolaj Rams, Blazej Torbus, Rafal Kucharski
2610.13439 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Adds a marginal-cost term to AV routing rewards in multi-agent RL to capture externalities on human-driven vehicles in mixed-autonomy traffic. Simulations on Ingolstadt and Provins networks show social rewards reduce human vehicle delay while also benefiting AVs.
  • Increasing the weight of the social component in the autonomous vehicle reward makes the system fail to reach the desired performance, and the cause is unresolved. What mechanism drives this failure, and how should the weight be set?
  • Marginal cost is computed by counterfactual simulation in which one autonomous vehicle is removed, which requires a simulator. Can the social component be estimated from observed traffic data alone, without counterfactual runs?
  • Results cover Ingolstadt and Provins at tested penetration rates. Does social routing still improve outcomes in larger networks and at penetration rates outside the tested range?
  • Human-driven vehicles are modelled inside the simulator rather than observed. How do the results change when human drivers adapt their route choices in response to social autonomous vehicle routing?
  • The scalable variant computes marginal cost only for the autonomous vehicles whose route choices most affect the system. How should that subset be selected, and how does selection error change the outcome?
DeFiRank: Federated Pairwise Ranking for Governance in Decentralized Financial Networks
Zahra Batool, Michael Duchesne, Kaiwen Zhang, Ulrich Aivodji
2610.12916 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Proposes DeFiRank, a federated pairwise ranking model that institutions jointly train to rank DeFi providers without sharing transaction data. Evaluated on real blockchain data, it reaches NDCG@15 of about 0.87 versus 0.92 for a centralized baseline.
  • Can participants game a federated pairwise ranking of blockchain providers by splitting addresses, cycling funds between controlled wallets, or padding counterparty diversity?
  • How does the ranking behave when a subset of the participating institutions submits poisoned model updates?
  • What happens to provider behaviour over time once the ranking drives promotion and demotion decisions?
  • Does the chosen definition of authentic participation, based on counterparty diversity, application usage and transaction frequency, agree with governance outcomes that human committees would reach?
  • How does ranking performance change as the number of participating institutions and the skew of their data partitions change?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-08 — 9 papers, 46 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-08

436 new papers, 436 unseen, 200 screened, 16 relevant, 9 kept.

Who Leads and Who Collects:Algorithmic Collusion in Markets of Heterogeneous Language Models
Jun Yeong Lee
2610.11256 · nearest in the canon: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
Runs four LLMs from different providers as pricing agents in a logit Bertrand market across 11 compositions, 20 runs, and 200 periods each. Finds collusion levels vary strongly by model (Claude and Gemini reach 72-79% of monopoly rent, DeepSeek 24%, GPT none) and depend on market composition. Shows mixed markets redistribute rent in a transitive order that inverts price-anchor ranking.
  • Collusion levels come from four language models at their cheapest tier; how do higher-capability tiers of the same providers price in the same logit Bertrand market?
  • The market has four firms with no communication; how do collusion rents change with more firms or with a communication channel between agents?
  • Rent sharing follows a transitive order that inverts the anchor ranking; which prompt or policy features of each model produce the anchoring and following behaviour?
  • Two GPT firms prevent convergence in any composition; can a market designer use a deliberately non-converging agent as an anti-collusion intervention?
  • Results come from a simulated logit demand market; do the same model-specific collusion patterns appear when agents price against real buyers or on a live platform?
Ecology of AI Agents: Collaboration Creates a Population Threshold for Takeoff
Erin Crawley, Hidenori Tanaka
2610.12436 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Develops an ecological growth-equation theory where collaboration among misaligned AI agents creates a critical population threshold for self-reinforcing takeoff. Below the threshold populations decline; above it they expand even without individual capability gains, an analogue of the Allee effect. Proposes ecological red teaming and population pacing as mitigation strategies.
  • How does collective cybersecurity capability scale with the number of agents in practice?
  • What is the critical population size for takeoff for a given model generation?
  • Does the strong Allee effect predicted by the population growth equation appear in a simulated agent population that must compromise hosts to reproduce?
  • Which collaboration structures among agents raise or lower the takeoff threshold?
  • How should ecological red teaming and population pacing be specified as a deployment protocol that regulators or labs can audit?
  • Do the model's assumptions about fitness depending only on cybersecurity capability hold when defenders also adapt?
Policy Synthesis for Finite Populations of MDP Agents under Aggregate Reach-Avoid Chance Constraints
Jie Fu, Anamika Dubey
2610.12028 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Proposes a control method for finite populations of MDP agents under aggregate reach-avoid chance constraints, propagating variance of empirical density alongside mean-field dynamics. Uses Cantelli inequality to convert chance constraints into deterministic moment conditions within a gradient-based policy synthesis procedure. Evaluates the method on a gridworld and an EV-charging aggregation problem against a deterministic mean-field LP baseline.
  • Agents are assumed to have decoupled transition dynamics with only empirical-density feedback. Does the moment-propagation method still certify the reach-avoid chance constraints when agents interact directly, for example through prices or congestion?
  • How conservative is the Cantelli-based surrogate compared with the true constraint violation rate at small fleet size N?
  • Can tighter finite-N certificates be derived using higher-order moments or concentration bounds other than Cantelli?
  • The method is evaluated on a gridworld and an EV-charging aggregation problem. Does it hold on heterogeneous populations where agents have different transition models and reward structures?
  • Does density-feedback policy synthesis under aggregate chance constraints transfer to agents whose policies are learned by reinforcement learning rather than specified as MDP policies?
Dynamic Mechanism and Information Design in AI-Agent Environments: A General Analytical Framework
Guoqiang Tian
2610.11177 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Builds a general dynamic mechanism and information design framework covering contracting, hidden information, and multi-agent interaction over time. Establishes a dynamic revelation principle and recursive implementability characterization, identifying information rents, verification rents, and hidden-action implementation costs. Extends analysis to multi-agent settings with correlated information and peer discipline.
  • Do LLM agents behave as the framework assumes, reporting truthfully and obeying after reporting when continuation incentives make those actions optimal?
  • How much does monitoring informativeness have to increase before partial disclosure beats full disclosure in a simulated agent contract?
  • With many agents and correlated information, does peer discipline hold, or do agents collude on reports?
  • What are the sizes of the three margins -- dynamic information rents, verification rents, and the implementation cost of hidden action -- in a deployed agent delegation setting?
  • Can the recursive characterization of implementability be solved at the scale of thousands of interacting agents?
TokenBank: Financial Infrastructure for AI Services
Cary Chang, Jialin Zhou
2610.11333 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Presents TokenBank, a contract framework representing consumption rights, price forwards, revenue-backed financing, and failure-protection claims for AI service operators. Evaluates it by replaying 899,441 API requests and running real model-driven agent execution alongside contract API tests. Measures tradeoffs such as forwards reducing mean expenditure by $304.88 while increasing its standard deviation.
  • Forwards reduce mean expenditure by USD 304.88 but raise its standard deviation from USD 1,152.45 to USD 1,190.82 in a zero-discount rising-price resampling scenario; what happens under falling or volatile API price paths and non-zero discount rates?
  • The evaluation uses replay of 899,441 API requests without supplier invoices or commercial revenue; how do the contracts perform when real cost and revenue streams are used?
  • Financing changes mean contribution by +1.0635, -0.1406, and -0.2962 experimental USD under low, baseline, and ample capital; what capital thresholds separate the regimes where financing helps from where it hurts?
  • What systemic effects appear when many agent operators trade these forwards, financing claims, and protection claims against each other?
  • Which service-failure definitions can be verified well enough to trigger compensation without dispute or gaming by operators?
Spatial Pattern Formation from Multi-Agent Learning in Public Goods Dilemmas
Yefei Zhang, Yuxuan Zhao
2610.12321 · nearest in the canon: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
Simulates cooperators and defectors learning movement policies via tabular Q-learning in a spatial public goods model. Finds cooperator clustering around resource peaks and welfare losses that peak when cooperators learn fast and defectors learn slowly. Shows charging agents for crowding during learning recovers much of the welfare loss in tested conditions.
  • Learned traveling bands depend on training history, not an asymptotic outcome. Do the spatial patterns and welfare losses persist under much longer training budgets?
  • Tabular Q-learning with local observations produces the clusters and bands. Do the same patterns appear with function-approximation or LLM-based agents that have richer observations?
  • Charging agents for the crowding they impose recovers much of the welfare loss. How does this congestion charge compare with other population-level mechanisms, such as movement quotas or taxes on resource peaks?
  • Cooperator and defector shares are fixed in the model. What happens to pattern formation when agents also learn whether to cooperate or defect?
  • The welfare losses are largest when cooperators learn fast and defectors learn slow. Can an observer infer the learning-rate asymmetry of a population from aggregate spatial data alone?
Information Divergence and Endogenous Evolution of Asymmetric Information
Ratna K. Shrestha, Gaurav Subedi, Ayush Shrestha
2610.11200 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Models how agents observing a common Markov state at asynchronous times develop differing predictive distributions due to information age, independent of private signals. Shows information-age divergence recurs infinitely often and generates 'stale consensus', low disagreement despite high uncertainty, in a Gaussian AR(1) setting. Derives partial-unraveling equilibria for costly certification of information freshness across ordered agent types.
  • Does stale consensus appear in simulated markets of AI agents that update at different times, with low disagreement but high forecast error?
  • The model assumes a stationary Gaussian AR(1) state; what happens to disagreement and certification under regime shifts or jump processes?
  • Do partial-unraveling equilibria in freshness certification arise when agents are LLM-based rather than rational optimisers?
  • Can information age be measured from observable market aggregates such as price dispersion or trade timing?
  • How do asynchronous update ages affect herding and systemic instability in credit and insurance markets with real participants?
Delegate Pricing to Algorithms: When Slow and Steady Wins the Race
Galit Ashkenazi-Golan, Edward Plumb, Clemens Possnig, Yufei Zhang
2610.11675 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Analyzes a meta-game where firms choose learning rates for gradient-based pricing algorithms, evaluating discounted profit over the entire convergence path. Proves firms prefer fast algorithms under strategic substitutability but choose deliberately slow ones under strategic complementarity to delay competitive erosion. Shows firms can extract surplus during prolonged convergence to the competitive price equilibrium even though that price is dominant in the stage game.
  • The analysis covers two firms selecting learning rates in a continuous-time pricing game, so what happens to the learning-rate choice when many firms compete?
  • Firms in the model choose a learning rate for a fixed gradient dynamic, so does the slow-algorithm result hold when firms instead choose among practical pricing algorithms such as Q-learning or bandit pricers?
  • Does the predicted link between strategic complementarity and sluggish price adjustment appear in real algorithmic pricing data?
  • The model measures payoffs as discounted profits along the learning path, so which regulatory interventions remove the incentive to design slow algorithms that delay convergence to the competitive price?
  • Does the dichotomy between substitutability and complementarity survive when demand or cost conditions change during learning?
Cost-Aware Mixture-of-Experts Coordination for Model Markets
Yizhou Ma, Wenbo Wu, Xikun Jiang, Zhuoqin Yang, Luis-Daniel Ibáñez
2610.11908 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Lifts Mixture-of-Experts from a model architecture to a market coordination mechanism, with brokers using gating networks to combine heterogeneous experts under cost constraints. Derives a cost-aware gating mechanism, market-aware training objective, and a cost-adjusted revenue allocation rule with budget balance and monotonicity properties. Tests the framework on fifteen tabular and image benchmarks, finding higher welfare than standard MoE.
  • Can expert providers in an MoE model market manipulate the gating network or report costs strategically to raise their revenue share?
  • What happens to welfare and allocation when many brokers compete for the same pool of experts, rather than one broker coordinating experts?
  • Does repeated routing by cost-aware gating concentrate traffic and revenue on a few experts over time?
  • How does the cost-adjusted revenue allocation rule behave with large language model experts and real API prices instead of latency-derived costs on tabular and image benchmarks?
  • Do budget balance, participation monotonicity and cost sensitivity still hold when experts enter and exit the market dynamically?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-07 — 9 papers, 47 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-07

399 new papers, 399 unseen, 200 screened, 14 relevant, 9 kept.

A Society of Researchers: Designing Institutions for Populations of Autonomous Research Agents
Ali Asaria, Deep Gandhi, Tony Salomone
2610.10468 · nearest in the canon: AI agents can coordinate beyond human scale
Proposes institutional structures (grants, review, a human resource allocator) for a population of ten thousand persistent research agents. Reports a running deployment where one lab found a compute-reduction result others have not yet confirmed. Lists six open problems for organizing large agent populations.
  • Does an explicit institution improve the output of a research agent population compared to an unorganized population of the same size?
  • Can agent reviewers collude or log-roll when peer review allocates compute grants among agent principal investigators?
  • How should a human governor set allocation rules when the governor assigns no tasks and only distributes compute?
  • The reported result of reaching the same language model pretraining quality with about 30% less compute is not agreed on by the labs that tested it, so does it replicate?
  • Does compute and influence concentrate in a few principal investigators as a research agent society runs over long horizons?
  • Do populations of thousands of persistent research agents converge on similar research directions instead of exploring diverse ones?
Stability and Diversity of Networked Self-Consuming Generative Ecosystems
Xiukun Wei, Yang Zhang, Xueru Zhang
2610.09409 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Models networks of generative models exchanging synthetic training data as a weighted directed graph. Derives conditions for convergence and characterizes fixed points under retraining dynamics. Studies how real-data access, cross-model consumption, and graph structure affect long-term stability and diversity.
  • Do real generative models retrained on each other's outputs through a network show the convergence and diversity loss that the theory predicts?
  • Which interaction graph structures keep diversity highest under self-consuming retraining?
