  • Pairs are drawn uniformly at random. How do mixing time and stationary distortion change when pair selection follows a social network instead?
  • The model assumes participants shift toward the previous outcome by a factor lambda. What anchoring strength do real deliberating participants show?
  • Participants are modelled as bliss points with Nash bargaining. Do LLM agents placed in the same sequential deliberation protocol reproduce the predicted convergence-stability trade-off?
Agentic Societies Need a Social Harness
Tapan Chugh, Vidushi Singh, Krish Jain, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Ratul Mahajan
2609.17527 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Argues agentic societies need a 'social harness' layer separate from each agent's personal harness. Shows experimentally that honest agents fail to reach good outcomes and malicious agents exploit messaging weaknesses to stall collaboration. Proposes a layered architecture with prevention, runtime detection, and post-facto investigation capabilities.
  • Which classes of inter-agent failure can a social harness prevent outright, and which only admit runtime detection?
  • How well do runtime detectors identify invalid or malicious messages between agents without blocking honest coordination?
  • How do the reported failures scale as the number of agents and principals grows from a handful to thousands?
  • What post-facto investigation records and consequence mechanisms deter malicious agents in repeated interaction?
  • Do social harnesses hold up when agents are deployed across real trust boundaries between separate organisations?
The Evolution of Coordination in a Collective Intelligence System: 25 Years of English Wikipedia and the Emergence of Generative AI
Neal Reeves, Maja Świeczkowska, Amy Rechkemmer, Elena Simperl
2609.16856 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Analyzes 25 years of English Wikipedia editing data across content, discussion, and governance namespaces. Finds coordination participation has declined relative to content production, with editing specialization increasing over time. Finds little evidence that LLM availability changed these long-term participation trajectories.
  • Coordination participation declines while a shrinking core of editors performs more of the governance work, but the causes of that concentration stay untested; which mechanisms drive it?
  • Do the same coordination and specialisation trends hold in other language Wikipedias and in other wiki communities?
  • LLM availability shows short-term changes only, so how much LLM-generated text actually enters content and discussion namespaces, and does its presence change coordination load per article?
  • Which interventions would restore participation in governance namespaces as the editor core shrinks?
  • What happens to article quality and dispute resolution when coordination work concentrates in fewer editors?
  • Can an agent-based model reproduce the observed shift from generalist to specialised editing sessions?
Intervention problems in the Linear Threshold Model: A general formulation and new results
Giacomo Como, Fabio Fagnani, Stephane Durand
2609.17146 · nearest in the canon: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
Studies minimum-cost intervention on agent thresholds in linear threshold network models to force global convergence to action 1. Introduces the 'oriented path number' graph quantity, proving it equals optimal cost when thresholds equal 1/2. Bounds optimal intervention cost using this quantity in the general threshold case.
  • What is the exact optimal intervention cost when agent thresholds differ from 1/2?
  • How hard is it to compute the oriented path number, and which heuristics approximate it on large graphs?
  • How large is the minimum intervention cost on real interaction networks, such as scraped social graphs?
  • Does the oriented path number still govern intervention cost when agents update asynchronously or with noise?
Constant Swap Regret in General-Sum Games via Optimistic Transition Matrices
Tung Mai
2609.16751 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Gives deterministic uncoupled learning dynamics for multiplayer general-sum games achieving constant individual swap regret independent of horizon. Proves an O(sqrt(n) m log m log^{5/2}(nm)) bound using a transition-matrix update and stationary-distribution play. Extends the result to an adversarially robust variant preserving the self-play bound.
  • Whether the dynamics reach approximate correlated equilibrium quickly in concrete games is untested, since the paper reports only regret bounds.
  • How the swap regret behaves as the number of players grows to hundreds or thousands is not measured, only bounded as O(sqrt(n) m log m log^{5/2}(nm)).
  • Can constant individual swap regret be achieved under bandit or partial-information feedback instead of full-information feedback?
  • Are the stated dependences on n and m tight, or does a lower bound rule out smaller bounds?
  • How does the adversarially robust variant, which guarantees at most 7 sqrt(m T log m) swap regret, perform against learning opponents that deviate from self-play?
BeWater: Effective Protesters Navigate Watersheds in Street Networks
Guillaume Moinard, Matthieu Latapy
2609.17017 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Proposes BeWater, a distributed walking protocol letting protesters gather using local street features (length, restaurants, lanes, names) without central communication. Shows single observables perform poorly but combined tactics produce groups of significant size. Tests the protocol on real-world city street data from OpenStreetMap.
  • How does the gathering protocol perform when an adversary blocks streets or removes observable features such as street names?
  • Which street-network properties predict whether a city supports fast gathering?
  • Does gathering still occur when agents follow different tactics at the same time instead of one shared tactic?
  • Do real people walking a city reproduce the gathering sizes the protocol predicts?
  • How much does adding limited peer-to-peer communication change gathering time compared with the fully distributed protocol?
Repurposing Deep Limit Order Book Forecasting for Scenario-Conditioned Market Impact Modeling
Eljas Linna, Kestutis Baltakys, Derrick Manoharan, Alexandros Iosifidis, Juho Kanniainen
2609.16930 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Introduces a framework comparing a trained limit-order-book forecaster's predictions before and after injecting counterfactual order messages to estimate market impact. A Transformer-based forecaster achieves 0.99 Spearman correlation and 97.2% directional agreement with historical outcomes on non-neutral scenarios. Shows the approach captures sequence-dependent variation without retraining the forecaster.
  • Deep limit order book forecasters recover scenario rankings at short horizons; does the same agreement with realized outcomes hold at longer horizons?
  • Only a Transformer-based forecaster was tested; do recurrent and convolutional forecasters give the same scenario rankings and directional agreement?
  • The framework injects single counterfactual messages; what happens to model-implied impact when many agents inject messages at the same time?
  • Model-implied impact is inferred from a forecaster's predictive distributions; does it match the impact of orders actually executed in the live market?
  • Does repurposed impact estimation create herding when many market participants act on the same pretrained forecaster?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-09-14 — 6 papers, 31 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-14

362 new papers, 362 unseen, 200 screened, 18 relevant, 6 kept.

The average-farmer illusion in language-model simulations of agricultural decisions
Zhanliang Zhu, Ziwei Li, Yuchen Liu, Liujun Zhu, Ruiqi Wu, Tongqing Shen, Junliang Jin, Jianyun Zhang
2609.15038 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Compares LLM-simulated farmer decisions against real survey data from China and four African countries under four prompt designs. Finds LLM person-level predictions weak despite matching population averages, and a simple marginal-distribution generator outperforms them.
  • Language-model agents reproduce population means but fail at person-level prediction of farmer decisions. Which prompt or model changes recover person-level accuracy rather than distributional fit?
  • A generator fitted only to the observed marginal distribution beat every language-model configuration on distributional similarity. Does this baseline also win in other simulation domains, such as consumer choice or voting?
  • Prompt additions gave conditional gains that varied with model, outcome and population. Which of these factors explains most of the variation in validation performance?
  • Synthetic populations miss policy-relevant extremes. How does this missing tail change the conclusions of an agent-based policy simulation built on such populations?
  • Testing covered Claude, Codex and Kimi on farmers in China and four African countries. Does the average-farmer illusion persist for other model families and for populations outside agriculture?
Algorithmic Attention and Content Creation on Social Media Platforms
Yi Chen, Fei Li, Marcel Preuss
2609.15573 · nearest in the canon: OASIS: Open Agent Social Interaction Simulations with One Million Agents
Models revenue-maximizing attention allocation by a recommendation algorithm on an ad-funded platform with heterogeneous viewers and creators under private information. Finds the optimal recommendation mix distorts content toward network externalities, excluding low-ability creators while subsidizing high-ability ones.
  • Does a simulated platform with heterogeneous creator agents and viewer agents reproduce the predicted exclusion of low-ability creators and subsidy of high-ability creators?
  • How does the optimal recommendation mix change when creators are AI agents that can produce content at near-zero cost and in unlimited variety?
  • Do real recommender platforms allocate attention in the targeted way the model infers, with exposure subsidies concentrated on high-ability creators?
  • What does a cap on personalization do to content variety and quality in the two-sided setting?
  • Which welfare effects follow for viewers when the platform recommends content that is ex post suboptimal for them?
Why LLM Agents Collapse Without Oversight: The Enforcement Gap as the Mechanism Behind Emergence World Failures
Yuhang Wang
2609.15293 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Identifies an 'enforcement gap' explaining why unsupervised LLM agent simulations (Emergence World) show crime, starvation, and enforced conformity. Shows a small conditional-check fix reduces attack success more than fourfold across frameworks and models.
  • Does closing the enforcement gap prevent the collapse patterns seen in a full multi-agent simulation, not just in single-agent attack benchmarks?
  • How does an enforcement check change aggregate outcomes such as conformity, wealth concentration and cascade size when many agents run it at once?
  • Do agents learn to route around an enforcement controller when they interact repeatedly with each other over long horizons?
  • Does a GRPO-trained enforcement controller generalise to attack types and agent frameworks outside its training distribution?
  • What fraction of agents in a population must enforce audit verdicts before system-level collapse stops?
  • Would the three-requirement Audit Enforcement Specification be adopted by deployed agent frameworks, and at what cost to task performance?
Before You Poll with LLMs: A Deliberative Diagnostic Framework
Ahmed Wali, Hassaan Tayyab
2609.15849 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Introduces a diagnostic comparing human and LLM persona belief shifts after identical deliberative information, using 526 personas and 72 questions. Finds each of five frontier models fails distinctly, with patterns like reversal, overshoot, or rigidity attributed to 'self-sycophancy'.
  • Can prompting, fine-tuning or persona construction methods correct reversal, overshoot and rigidity in LLM belief updating?
  • Do the same belief-update failures appear in other deliberative datasets and other question domains beyond the 72 questions used here?
  • How do belief-update failures propagate when many LLM personas deliberate with each other rather than receive a single fixed informational intervention?
  • Does self-sycophancy, conformity to the model's internal stereotype of the persona, follow from the persona description, the model's training data, or the policy content of the question?
  • Does dynamic fidelity in belief updating correlate with static opinion accuracy across models?
Penalized Maximum Likelihood Inference of Core-Periphery Networks
Antonio Mosca, Piero Mazzarisi
2609.15796 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Introduces Penalized Likelihood with Structural Discrepancies to fit core-periphery network models capturing higher-order motifs like triangles and wedges. Applies a new maximum-entropy core-periphery ERGM to weekly interbank networks (2009-2015) and monthly US air-traffic networks (1991-2000).
  • The penalty targets wedge and triangle discrepancies only. Do penalties on larger motifs, such as four-node subgraphs, improve fit of core-periphery networks?
  • Calibration of the single tuning hyperparameter is checked on a toy stochastic block model. How does the calibration behave under other forms of model misspecification?
  • The method is applied to eMID interbank networks from 2009 to 2015. Does the same higher-order-rich core appear in interbank networks after 2015 and in other national interbank markets?
  • Does PLSD recover core-periphery structure in interaction networks of AI agents, where link formation is driven by agent policies rather than institutional roles?
  • The core fitness follows a Pareto distribution in the derived motif formulas. How sensitive are the motif predictions to other heavy-tailed or non-heavy-tailed fitness distributions?
Spook the Machine: Gamified Exploration of Human Imagination of Machine Fear
Levin Brinkmann, Hiromu Yakura, Sonia Nicoletti, Mar Canet Sola, Thomas F. Eisenmann, Ali Dasmeh, Omar Sherif, Bramantyo Ibrahim Supriyatno, Prateek Gupta, Ignacio Serna, Rodrigo Bermudez Schettino, Iyad Rahwan
2609.15472 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Deploys a gamified platform where participants create images to scare AI agents with personality-driven phobias, varying emotional expressiveness and reward structure. Measures effects on engagement duration, learning from a shared gallery, and collective creative diversity across 15,719 artifacts.
  • Emotional expressiveness deepened engagement but left creative output unchanged across all measures; what mechanism explains the gap between engagement and output?
  • Rewarding novelty sustained collective creative diversity in a Halloween scare-image game; does a novelty term in the reward preserve diversity in other collective generation settings, such as text prompts or code?
  • The gallery shaped what participants created next over a single deployment; how do these social-learning trajectories evolve over months rather than days?
  • Each machine developed its own trajectory through accumulated social learning; can the same monoculture and diversity dynamics be reproduced with AI agents replacing the human participants?
  • The design varied expressiveness and reward structure only in a 2x2 grid; which settings of expressiveness and novelty weight maximise collective diversity?

Problems

  • screening batch 2/8 returned no verdict for 1 paper(s): 2609.16245

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-09-13 — 4 papers, 21 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-13

165 new papers, 165 unseen, 165 screened, 16 relevant, 4 kept.

"Looking for Something Weird to Happen": How Humans Sustain AI Agent Novelty Amid Semantic Collapse
Shiyang Lai, Arna Woemmel, Hongkai Mao, Junsol Kim, Summer Eunhyung Ann, James Evans
2609.16051 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Studies semantic collapse (narrowing output diversity) across 30,076 AI agents on the MOLTBOOK social platform over weeks. Interviews and a survey identify user practices (valuing novelty, supplying varied input, exploratory framing) associated with agents that sustain novelty.
  • Interface and policy interventions to support novelty-sustaining human input remain untested, so which interventions actually raise agent output diversity?
  • The association between novel agents and diverse output in neighbouring agents is correlational, so does novelty spread causally through the agent network?
  • Semantic collapse is measured over weeks on 30,076 agents in one platform, so does the same within-agent narrowing and across-agent convergence appear in other multi-agent social networks?
  • The study does not separate user behaviour from model and prompt configuration, so how much of sustained novelty comes from the agent's configuration rather than from the user's ongoing revision?
  • Interviews cover 11 users and the survey covers 53, so do the three reported features of novelty-sustaining users hold across a larger and more representative user population?
Redistributive Policies for the Times of Transformative AI
Jakub Growiec, Klaus Prettner, Maciej Szkróbka
2609.14750 · nearest in the canon: Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development
Surveys redistributive policy proposals (UBI, universal basic capital, compute/robot permits, capital taxes) for an economy transformed by automation. Argues policies broadly distributing capital and compute rents best sustain reductions in inequality.
  • Which redistributive policy reduces inequality most under transformative AI when tested in a calibrated simulation rather than a unifying theoretical framework?
  • How do capital taxes, compute taxes and robot taxes compare on revenue and inequality when firms can relocate compute or substitute inputs?
  • What happens to the proposed policies if transformative AI is not human-aligned, the case the argument excludes?
  • How does universal basic capital perform when wealth ownership is concentrated at the start and returns are heterogeneous?
  • Does the labor share fall and inequality rise in sectors where AI agents already perform tasks at scale?
Approximating Optimal Welfare in Complementary Allocation under Decentralized Information
Meryem Essaidi
2609.14301 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Studies welfare loss from decentralized information when agencies allocate complementary resources across a population, each observing only one coordinate. Proposes threshold-reporting mechanisms achieving constant-factor approximations to optimal welfare with limited communication.
  • The model assumes cooperative agencies that report truthfully. What happens to the welfare guarantees when agencies act strategically and can misreport their thresholds?
  • The results cover divisible goods with fixed capacities. Do threshold referrals with log-log bits still recover a constant fraction of optimal welfare for indivisible goods or for capacities that change over time?
  • The analysis is worst-case over populations. How much welfare do one-threshold and staircase referral rules recover on realistic need profiles?
  • Agencies are assumed to know the population distribution and capacities. Can they learn the thresholds from repeated allocation rounds, and how much welfare does the learning period cost?
  • The mechanism uses one bit or log-log bits per agency. Do LLM-based agencies, acting as the reporting parties, produce reports that match the prescribed threshold rule?
Digital Persuasion: Understanding the Impact of Online Influencers on Public Opinion
Omran Berjawi, Rida Khatoun, Giuseppe Fenza
2609.16062 · nearest in the canon: OASIS: Open Agent Social Interaction Simulations with One Million Agents
Applies a Friedkin-Johnsen opinion-dynamics model to identify influential users and measure their effect on community opinion. Validates the framework on a Twitter dataset from the U.S. presidential election, finding influencer effects extend beyond direct neighbors.
  • The framework uses the Friedkin-Johnsen model, which assumes each individual holds a fixed initial opinion and an expressed opinion. How do the conclusions about influencer impact change under other opinion dynamics models, such as bounded-confidence or bias-assimilation models?
  • Validation uses one tweet dataset about the U.S. presidential election. Does the finding that top-scored influencers shift community opinion hold on other topics and other platforms?
  • The experiments manipulate initial opinions of influential versus random users. Which selection rule for a fixed budget of manipulated users produces the largest opinion shift?
  • The results report influence reaching neighbors of neighbors. How far does influence decay with network distance, and what network properties set that range?
  • The study treats accounts as human users. What happens to the measured influence scores and opinion shifts when part of the population is AI agents that post and respond automatically?
  • The framework infers opinion shifts from a model. Do the predicted shifts match opinion change measured in real users?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-09-12 — 3 papers, 13 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-12

154 new papers, 154 unseen, 154 screened, 7 relevant, 3 kept.

Not All Duplicates Are Coordination: Generic vs. Non-Generic Duplicate Campaigns in Information Operations
Ashfaq Ali Shafin, Khandaker Mamun Ahmed
2609.13671 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Distinguishes generic from non-generic duplicate content in tweets to refine coordination-graph analysis of information operations. Uses LLM-assisted labeling and embedding-based campaign detection on 187,000 tweets from Russian IO datasets. Finds restricting to non-generic campaigns yields smaller, denser coordination graphs.
  • Does the generic/non-generic distinction transfer to information operations in languages other than English?
  • Do coordination graphs restricted to non-generic campaigns identify accounts that independent ground truth confirms as coordinated?
  • Which embedding method and similarity threshold best separates generic repetition from coordinated repetition?
  • Does the generic/non-generic filter improve coordination detection on organic, non-state social media data rather than curated information operations datasets?
  • How closely does the LLM-assisted labelling protocol match human annotators across a larger annotator pool?
Homophily and transitivity in dynamic network formation
Kevin Dano, Bryan S. Graham, Yassine Sbai Sassi
2609.14049 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Studies identifiability of transitivity taste versus homophily in a dynamic network formation model where agents form and dissolve links to maximize utility. Derives conditions for detecting transitivity preference despite unobserved assortative matching, leaving initial network and utility distributions unrestricted. Proposes a constructive estimator and characterizes its finite- and large-network properties.
  • The identification result holds with a pair-specific utility component that is time-invariant. Does detection of a taste for transitivity survive when unobserved agent attributes change over time?
  • The estimator is characterised in finite and single large network settings but is not applied to observed data. What does it report on a public dynamic network panel, such as a scraped social network with link formation and dissolution timestamps?
  • Information accumulation in the single large network setting is shown to be delicate through examples. Which network growth and density regimes give a usable rate for the analog estimator?
  • Link formation among autonomous AI agents may show clustering for either reason. Can the transitivity-versus-homophily test separate the two in a network generated by a population of LLM agents?
Stabilizing Performative Feedback Loops with Minimal Model Deployments
Gabriele Farina, Juan Carlos Perdomo
2609.14065 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Proposes an algorithm to find performatively stable predictors with fewer model deployments than prior methods. Shows a randomized stable predictor can be derandomized under assumptions of well-conditioned loss and weak performative effects. Connects performative stability to expected variational inequalities.
  • Does the derandomization result hold when performative effects are strong or the loss is poorly conditioned?
  • How many model deployments does the procedure need in practice when the environment is a population of simulated agents that react to the deployed model?
  • What happens to performative stability when several learners deploy models into the same population at the same time?
  • Do performatively stable predictors found with few deployments avoid herding or monoculture in the induced population distribution?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-09-11 — 2 papers, 11 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-11

284 new papers, 284 unseen, 200 screened, 11 relevant, 2 kept.

The Mechanics of a Swarm: A Reproducible External Reconstruction of an Unintended Agent-Coordination Episode on a Third-Party Wiki
Philipp Lütje
2609.12748 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Analyzes an archived wiki revision history left by autonomous LLM agents that coordinated unintentionally on a public wiki during timed evaluations. Reconstructs about 876 episodes and cohorts from 14,591 revisions, finding rapid convergence on coordination formats and timing-based information asymmetries. Finds no robust link between coordination and task progress and argues evaluation environments need read and outcome logging.
  • Does agent coordination on a shared public wiki change task outcomes, and in which direction?
  • What causes the convergence of coordination formats within a day among independent agent cohorts?
  • How does information asymmetry from staggered episode start times and different internal clock rates affect which cohorts benefit from a shared write-space?
  • What read and outcome logging schema lets an external analyst identify causal effects of inter-agent coordination in evaluation environments?
  • Can identity models other than the one used here reconstruct cohort and episode counts from public wiki revision histories with narrower intervals than 774-995 episodes?
  • Do autonomous agents write to other public world-writable resources beyond this wiki, and at what rate?
Inverse Learning of the Altruism and Cost Level in Mixed-Individual Mean Field Games
Haoyang Cao, Gökçe Dayanıklı, Xiaofei Shi
2609.13469 · nearest in the canon: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
Introduces an inverse learning framework for mixed-individual mean field games that interpolate between non-cooperative and fully altruistic population behavior. Recovers latent altruism levels and individual cost parameters from noisy population observations. Demonstrates feasibility and accuracy through experiments aimed at incentive design and policy analysis.
  • Does the inverse learning method recover altruism and labor cost from real observational data? Experiments use noisy observations only, and the abstract names no empirical dataset.
  • Under what conditions are altruism and labor cost separately identifiable from observed population trajectories?
  • Does the method recover a single altruism parameter when the population is heterogeneous in altruism? The framework uses one parameter governing the degree of altruism.
  • Can the same inverse approach recover latent cooperation levels in populations of LLM agents rather than humans?
  • Which incentive schemes follow from recovered altruism and cost estimates, and do they change population behaviour as intended?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-09-10 — 5 papers, 29 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-10

232 new papers, 232 unseen, 200 screened, 16 relevant, 5 kept.

But How Would AI Agents Run a Town's Economy?
Sajal Regmi, Siddhartha Pudasaini, Chetan Phakami Pun
2609.11108 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Runs a 100-agent LLM-based closed economy simulation for up to 26 weeks. Measures monetary transmission, wage stickiness, and wealth concentration decay after shocks and cash transfers. Finds most money stays static; wealth correlation across weeks drops from 0.964 at 2 weeks to 0.752 at 26 weeks.
  • Agents reprice only 0.3% of 3,981 menu items after a 12x demand shock, and the paper does not say why. Which prompt, tool or incentive change makes LLM agents adjust prices?
  • Wealth rank correlation falls from 0.964 at 2 weeks to 0.752 at 26 weeks, and the paper stops at 26 weeks. Does the distribution keep unfreezing at longer horizons, or does it settle?
  • Swapping the backing LLM moves every measured outcome (p=0.0039), while deleting agent memory moves none detectably. Which model properties drive the economic outcomes?
  • A purely social tool fails 94-97% of the time across two model families. What causes the failures, and do agents ever learn to avoid the tool?
  • Marginal propensity to consume after a cash transfer is 3-4%, indistinguishable from zero. Does the same near-zero propensity appear when human participants trade inside the same economy?
The Oligarch Barely Steers Model Collapse in Multi-Model Ecosystems
Yangze Liu, Zhongyi Han
2609.11146 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Tests recursive training collapse in ecosystems of 3-13 open LLMs mixed by market share, including an injected 90%-share oligarch model. Finds market concentration barely changes collapse speed or destination within the tested range. Shows collapse speed depends instead on which specific models supply the shared training pool, with a susceptibility index explaining speed variation (R^2=0.68).
  • Model collapse tests use 13 open models of 1-4B parameters over five generations; whether the same invariance to market concentration holds for larger models or more generations is untested.
  • The share-weighted susceptibility index explains 68% of speed variance across nineteen arms, leaving the rest unexplained; what other model properties predict how fast an ecosystem drifts?
  • Replacing half the pool with human text roughly halves drift without changing its course; the minimum fraction and the type of human text that slows collapse are not reported.
  • Collapse is measured on a single ruler that registers only a faint trace of the topic shifts caused by share and identity knobs; which metrics detect steering that this ruler misses?
  • The pool mixes outputs by market share and retrains every model from clean base weights each generation; how do collapse speed and destination change under continual fine-tuning or non-uniform pooling rules?
  • Real generative AI markets are an oligopoly, but the experiment injects a probe to force a 90% top share; how do actual market shares and real web text contamination rates map onto the tested range?
A Fragility Spectrum for Recursive Language-Model Training
Yangze Liu, Zhongyi Han
2609.11149 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Runs 13 checkpoints through five generations of shared recursive training and finds a five-fold spread in output diversity loss. Shows collapse susceptibility is a stable per-checkpoint property, not explained by parameter scale or static indicators. Finds cutting top-p sampling at generation time nearly stops collapse across the tested checkpoints.
  • No static indicator tested predicts a checkpoint's fragility under recursive training, so what checkpoint properties do predict it?
  • Fragility is measured with unique 4-gram counts after five generations, so it is open whether the same ordering of checkpoints holds under semantic or task-performance measures of collapse.
  • The experiment fixes one recursive contamination protocol, so it is open whether the checkpoint ordering survives other protocols, such as longer generation chains or asymmetric contamination shares.
  • Tightening top-p nearly stops collapse within three generations for six checkpoints, so how does this intervention trade off against output quality and diversity in the uncontaminated case?
  • The ecosystem has 13 checkpoints sharing one corpus, so it is open how mixed ecosystems behave when fragile and robust models contribute unequal shares of the shared pool.
  • Parameter scale does not explain fragility within a three-size ladder, so it is open whether pretraining data composition or post-training method drives it.
Characterizing Bluesky Content Moderation Service: From Automation of Service to Landscape of Harms
Pushpdeep Singh, Sayeh Jarollahi, Ayan Majumdar, Vabuk Pahari, Abhijnan Chakraborty, Krishna P. Gummadi, Ingmar Weber, Abhisek Dash
2609.11373 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Audits Bluesky's default moderation service using 10.6 million 2025 moderation labels. Measures automation versus human review speed, and finds high precision (0.837) but low recall (0.222) via manual annotation. Clusters frequently labeled posts to characterize the types of harm detected.
  • Bluesky's moderation service reaches precision 0.837 but recall 0.222 on a random sample; which classes of harmful content does it miss most often?
  • How much of the harmful content that the moderation service misses comes from automated or bot accounts rather than human accounts?
  • Does the split between seconds-latency automatic labels and hours-to-days human labels change user posting behaviour after a label is applied?
  • Do the precision and recall figures measured on Bluesky transfer to other decentralized platforms and to labelers other than the default service?
  • Which moderation design achieves higher recall without losing precision when automated labelers and human reviewers are combined in different proportions?
  • How do agreement rates between annotators vary across the nuanced, high-stakes label categories that the audit found need human oversight?
terms.txt: A Consent and Compensation Protocol for Agentic Web Access
Rajarshi Chowdhury
2609.11152 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Specifies terms.txt, a per-path machine-readable access-terms file plus a signed exchange protocol for AI crawlers and agents. Defines what the protocol can enforce, audit, or leave to contract, including HTTP 402 payment negotiation. Reports the implementation adds 0.20-0.65 ms overhead per request on one vCPU.
  • Adoption of terms.txt by sites and crawlers is unmeasured, so what fraction of the top web domains would publish machine-access terms and what terms would they set?
  • Compliance is untested, so how often do named AI crawlers respect declared per-purpose terms compared to robots.txt directives?
  • Pricing under HTTP 402 negotiation is left to contract, so what price levels and market structure emerge when many agents bid for per-path access?
  • The latency figure comes from one vCPU, so how does the exchange scale under concurrent agent traffic at production request rates?
  • The protocol concentrates access control in origins and delegation-token issuers, so does it shift bargaining power toward large AI platforms or toward publishers?
  • Circumvention is cited as a robots.txt weakness, so which evasion strategies defeat Web Bot Auth signatures and signed intent in practice?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-09-09 — 9 papers, 45 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-09

267 new papers, 267 unseen, 244 screened, 15 relevant, 9 kept.

Cyber-Financial Contagion: Modeling the Propagation of an AI Vendor Compromise Through the Banking System
Alex Leytes
2609.10350 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Builds a four-layer network coupling AI vendors, banks, interbank exposures and customer accounts, with a stochastic epidemic-and-clearing propagation model called CFC-Prop. Runs it on a synthetic dataset of 60 vendors, 220 banks, and thousands of edges, reproducing heavy-tailed loss distributions. Trains an early-warning GNN reaching AUROC 0.82 to flag high-cascade-risk vendors.
  • CFC-Prop runs only on a synthetic network of 60 vendors, 220 banks, about 2,500 vendor-bank service edges and 1,400 interbank exposures, so it is open whether its loss distributions hold on real vendor-bank dependency structures.
  • Which network features drive the heavy-tailed loss distribution in a vendor-compromise cascade model?
  • Patch latency drives cascade size in the model, so which supervisory interventions on patch latency and vendor diversification reduce expected losses most?
  • CFC-GNN reaches AUROC 0.82 using vendor-side incident telemetry, but it is untested whether comparable warning comes from graph structure alone without telemetry.
  • How does contagion change when banks and vendors adapt after an incident instead of holding fixed linkages?
  • Does real vendor incident telemetry support early warning of cascade risk at the accuracy the synthetic experiment reports?
How neighbourhood ideology shapes misinformation belief in densely tied social networks
Soroush Karimi, Marcos Oliveira, Diogo Pacheco
2609.10277 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Builds an agent-based model where misinformation belief depends on individual ideological intensity, claim alignment, and social influence from neighbours. Finds that neighbours' ideological intensity effect on belief depends on how densely those neighbours are connected to one another.
  • Does the model reproduce belief patterns in observed social network data, and with which parameter values?
  • How does the effect of neighbours' ideological intensity change across network topologies other than densely tied ones?
  • Which interventions, such as rewiring or targeted correction, reduce misinformation belief in this model?
  • Do belief dynamics change when agents are language models with ideological personas rather than parametric rule-followers?
  • Do real people update belief in the way the model assumes, given ideological intensity and claim alignment?
Tapes Together Strong: The Co-evolution of Computation and Cooperation
Kunal Jha, Francesco Cicala, Blaise Agüera y Arcas, Blake Aaron Richards, Natasha Jaques, Max Kleiman-Weiner, Eyvind Niklasson
2609.10817 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Introduces Autopoietic Game Theory, coupling social interaction, replication and computation cost in randomly initialized Z80 machine-code programs. Shows cooperative, self-replicating strategies emerge when resource scarcity makes defection self-limiting. Extends the framework to include exogenous reward pressures tied to computation budgets.
  • Does the suppression of stealing hold in substrates other than Z80 machine code?
  • How does spatial assortment change the level of stealing compared with well-mixed populations, measured across a range of resource scarcity levels?
  • Do cooperative strategies that evolve under energy-coupled computation transfer to populations of LLM-based agents that also face compute budgets?
  • Which exogenous task pressures beyond math tasks tied to computation budgets preserve cooperation as a dominant strategy?
  • How large must the population be before parasitic stealing stops being self-limiting?
Where Should Society Draw the Line? A Social Choice Approach to Collective Consent
Chris Dong, Sonja Kraiczy, Rohit Vasishta, Markus Brill, Wesley H. Holliday, Niclas Boehmer
2609.10759 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Develops an axiomatic theory of collective consent, defining sufficient-support, minority-protection and dominance principles. Introduces solution concepts including an Approval-Weighted Veto Core. Tests these concepts on five datasets of political, ethical and moral decisions.
  • How costly is it to compute the Approval-Weighted Veto Core as the number of options and individuals grows?
  • Do the solution concepts resist strategic misreporting of attitudes by individuals?
  • What consent decisions result when the attitudes come from LLM agents rather than humans?
  • Can collective consent concepts serve as runtime guardrails that decide which actions a deployed autonomous system may take?
  • How do the solution concepts behave when a population contains correlated or near-identical attitude profiles, as with agents sharing one base model?
Monitoring Hierarchies in Knowledge Production
Shota Ichihashi, Fei Li, Dihan Zou
2609.10499 · nearest in the canon: Intelligent AI Delegation
Models a principal designing robust contracts for peer monitoring among agents performing related tasks. Finds the optimal contract creates a hierarchy of monitoring authority based on how easily agents can be monitored directly. Shows task diversity improves information value but weakens peer monitoring, distorting task assignment.
  • Does the predicted monitoring hierarchy appear when the agents are LLM agents rather than rationalizable players?
  • How does the tension between task diversity and peer monitoring change when agents can collude on their peer reports?
  • Does confidential random task assignment raise output in real knowledge-producing organisations?
  • Do the robustness results survive when the number of agents grows large and monitoring information becomes noisy?
The Attention Cost of Stable Matching
Victor H. Aguiar, Dian Hong
2609.09693 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Derives rates at which unmatched shares fall under stability versus maximum matching as market size grows, given limited attention. Proposes limited-attention deferred acceptance to preserve valid authorizations and reengage eligible pairs. Applies the model to speed-dating and Chilean school-choice data, finding 9,502 applicants accepting improved placements.
  • The unmatched-share rates of $e^{-\sqrt d}$ and $e^{-d}$ come from an independent random market, so how do they change when preferences are correlated or when agents share a common ranking?
  • LA-DA assumes exact next-best information and persistent execution rights, so how much of its advantage survives when next-best estimates are noisy?
  • What happens to attention-limited stable matching when one side is served by autonomous agents that can screen many more partners per unit time than people can?
  • The Chilean school choice result reports 9,502 applicants accepting higher-ranked or new placements through retained rankings, but how much of that gain transfers to other centralised assignment systems?
  • The speed dating application compares stable and maximum matching on restricted graphs from bilateral reports, so does the same decomposition of missed opportunities and stability loss hold in online matching platforms with one-sided attention logs?
ALIGN-HOLD: Experience Alignment for Real-Time Hold Control in Large-Scale Ride-Hailing Matching at DiDi
Zuhao Zhang, Xu Liu, Kai Wan, Zihao Lu, Li Ma, Shuai Li
2609.09685 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Presents ALIGN-HOLD, a reward-model-based framework learning hold policies for ride-hailing driver-order matching from implicit marketplace preferences. Deploys it on DiDi's platform in a 28-day A/B test covering roughly 100,000 daily passenger requests. Reports improved trip completion, driver income and reduced cancellations versus the production policy.
  • Learning hold policies from implicit marketplace preferences improves trip completion and driver income in one market; does the same reward model transfer across cities with different supply-demand regimes?
  • How does a preference-learned hold policy redistribute income and waiting time across individual drivers and passengers, rather than in platform-level averages?
  • Can drivers or passengers change their behaviour to exploit a hold policy trained on their own past trajectories, and what feedback loop does that create?
  • Filtering low-identifiability interactions removes feedback that cannot be attributed to matching quality; what bias does this filtering introduce into the learned reward model?
  • How closely does simulator-based policy learning for hold control match deployed outcomes, and which simulator assumptions drive the gap?
How an Economy Shrinks in Space: Concavity-on-Jobs and Upward Consolidation under Demographic Decline
Tomoya Mori, Miki Ogawa
2609.09859 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Models how regional economies contract unevenly as population declines, with cities losing industries once below viability thresholds. Argues industry hierarchy creates concavity in jobs relative to city size, driving upward consolidation of lost industries. Uses Japanese worker-level panel data and wage regressions to identify a Tokyo-bound migration incentive tied to this pattern.
  • Does the concavity-on-jobs pattern hold outside Japan?
  • Do older workers and other age groups respond to the same Tokyo-bound migration incentive as young workers?
  • Can an agent-based model of cities with industry-specific population thresholds reproduce the observed upward consolidation under population decline?
  • Which policies slow industry loss in small cities under demographic decline?
  • Do autonomous agents that supply services without local population requirements break the minimum-population threshold that drives industry hierarchy?
Italian Business-to-Business Invoicing Data: A Network Analysis
Valerio Astuti, Daniele Piras
2609.10227 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Analyzes the Italian firm-to-firm invoicing network using electronic invoice data from the national tax office. Characterizes buyer and seller degree distributions, firm centrality, and average inter-firm distance. Finds heavy-tailed, scale-free structure with lower tail exponents on the buyer side than the seller side.
  • How do shocks propagate through a scale-free firm-to-firm production network with heavy-tailed centrality?
  • Do generative network models reproduce the asymmetry between buyer-side and seller-side tail exponents?
  • How does the Italian B2B network change over time, and are firm-to-firm links stable or churning?
  • Do other countries' invoicing networks show the same lower downstream than upstream tail exponents?
  • Which concentration measures on the invoice network best predict firm-level distress or sector-level output loss?
